BY PRIVATE POST. From a white-winged ship in a far-off bay, 'Mid halcyon isles of the blue southern seas, A dark headed face oft looks fondly this was, And wafts to his Mecca a sigh on the breeze. My letters to him go by sixpenny post; But then there is something he sadly will miss, Because the bonne bouche he would care for the most They cannot convey. Can you guess? It's a kiss! So I keep my own pillar-box. You never saw A prettier Cupid, more perfect design; A statuette rosy, a gem without flaw, Bedimpled and beautiful—almost divine. I've just washed my dear little boy for the night, 'fhen—sweet broken music—he babbled his prayers; ills body and soul are anew clean and white, Just like Jacob's angels ascending the stairs. Who can tell whither his spirit may roam, When once those soul•windows are curtained in sleep; perchance it may float in the star-spangled dome, Or fly to his father far over the deep. For love laughs at locksmiths, defies bolts and bars, The bounds of its pinions no mortal can tell, It soars with the seraphs, outwinging the stars, It won back Eurydice even from hell. And So, full of faith, they shall reach him somehow— I send nightly kisses away to the 6outh, My choicest ones, meant for my dear husband's brow, By Love's own post-office, my baby-boy's mouth. .--Good Woris. Giro RGE Flax,.

Reform, like charity, must begin at home. -If rich, be not elated; if poor, be not dejected. He is a wise man who rnakei to-morrow from to-day. A handful of good life is worth a bmihel of learning. The detective has his "dog days all the year round. Trtfles light as hair sometimes turn :the whole course of a man's appetite. "What's that ?" "That's a kaleidoscope." "Is it? When does it begln to colider Yea of character are the conscience of the society to which they belong. A weak mind is like a microscope, which magnifies trifling thines, but cannot receive great ones. Feelings are always made the excuse of temper; whereas temper much more frequently influences feeling. First boy (to second boy, who: has been fishing) : "Catch anything ?" Second boy: "I haven't been home yet." "Can nothing more be None for the prisoner, Mr. Brief ?" "I fear not, sir." "The legal expedients are all exhausted, are they ?" "No, but the prisoner's money is." "I don't believe that like cures like." "Can you dis- prove it ? " "I can. My peace of mind is not improved by a piece of rnyf wife's mind." Moral principles are social and universal. They form, in a manner, the party of human-kind against vice and disorder, its common enemy. flouour is like the eye, which cannot suffer the least impurity without damage; it is a precious stone, the price of which is lessened by the least flaw. "Is that cement any good ?" asked a prospective pur- chaser of a pedlar. "Any good!!" was the reply. "Why, you could mend the break of day with that cement" Snooper: "It's no wonder they are always finding microbes, bacteria, and such things in France." Simeral : " Why ? " Snooper: "Because France is just the place for Parisites." Miss Passe° (examining medal of a recent graduate): "I have a medal, too."_ _Young Friend "you have?

May: "Well, I'm glad that for once in your life you've stuck to yourwork." Mrs. White: "I'm afraid Johnny won't drink that sarsaparilla if I tell him what it is. and if I give it to him without telling he'll be suspicious." Mrs. Brown: "Hide it away in the corner of the pantry. He's sure to drink it then."

A little three-year-old girl went to a children's party one afternoon. On her return she said to her parents:— At the party a little girl fell through a chair to the floor. All the other girls laughed, but I didn't." "Well, why didn't you laugh?" "'Cause I was the one that fell through." " Mr. Jerrold," said a lady, "I cannot imagine what makes my hair turn gray. I sometimes fancy it must be the essence of roseinarr with which my maid is in the, habit of brushing it. What do you think ?" "I should be rather afraid, madam," replied the distinguished Douglas, "that it must be 'the essence of time.'" Bridget O'Rafferty : "As if I'd take your notis: to l'ave ; thim days of slay'ry be past." Mr. Van de Vere : "This day month—." Bridget: "No, ma'am, excuse me—l've j'ined the Dames ;of Labour, :and I'll . . . .

just be afther callite in Miss:M‘Ginnis, what does the washin' next door, and Miss O'Flaherty, what scrubs 'round the corner, to arbithrate betwane us." A lay paper has been libelling the craft as follows : Boy (hurriedly) : "Gimme a bottle of Dr. Quacker's cough syrup, Mr. Squills." : "Five shillings, please." Boy (reproachfully) :7." Now lj This ain't for a customer; it's for Mr. Menthol at: the corner. l'm the boy in his shop." Squills: "Oh ! excuse:me, I thought yonlwere the public. Ninepence, please." While escorting a lady home, the other evening, a country doctor attempted to,relieve hersourth and sore throat by giving her a cough lozenge. He told her to allow it to dissolve gradually in her mouth. No relief was experienced; and the doctor felt quite chagrined the next day when the lady sent him a coat button, with a note, saying that he must have given her the wrong kind of lozenge, and that he might need the one that she Iliad enclosed. While cross-examining Dr. Warren, a New York toun.sel declared that a doctor ought to be able to give an opinion of a disease without making mistakes. '4They make fewer mistakes than the lawyers," re- sponded the physician. "That's noeso," said the coun- Bellor • "but doetors' mistakes are buried six feet under- ground, a lawyer's are not." "No." replied Warren, •" but they are sometimes hung as many as twelve feet . above ground." ; Nlaxtxu PRACE.—Simple words are best, though a • very busy man cannot always stop to pick one. At an hotel a waiter came out of the coffee-room and informed - the manager that a man was raising a disturbance be- cause he could not have his accustomed seat at the table. "Go in again," said the manager, "and pro- pitiate him in some way." Back went the waiter, and " If you don't like th- way things is done here, you can get out, or I'll propitiate you pretty quick." Dr. Moor, Professor of Greek in Glasgow, W9k a rather natty as well as a learned mau—that l to say, he was] particular in the cut of his dreg.% atIO. most particular to I the curl and powder °t his 'wig. Strutting about One day, as he was wont-, *Apparently well pleased with his . own appearante, he was noticed by a young spark of an 'officer, long in commission, who, thinking to annoy 'the 1-.olessor, whispered to his companion in passing, Jud enough, however, for the Doctor to hear, "He smells strongly of powder." Upon which the Doctor at once turned round and said, "Don't be alarmed, my brave young soldier; it is not gun-powder!" "THERE, MY LORD, I LEAVE You !" —ln mean lodg- ings over a shop close by the entrance to Spring Gardense 1 which down to our own times was a saddler's, died the celebrated divine and preacher, Dr. Isaac Barrow, one of the most illustrious scholars and writers ; and his Wit has been spoken of by no less an authority than Dr. , Johnson, as "the finest thing in the language." We quote an instance of the doctor's ready wit. In meeting the Earl of Rochester one day, the worthy peer ,7ex- claimed, "Doctor, I am yours to the shoe tie ; ' to which the clergyman replied, ' My lord, I am yours to the ground." The peer rejoined, " Doctor, lam yours to the centre." "My lord, " retorted the doctor, "I am yours to the antipodes." Determined not to be outdone, his lordship blasphemously added," Doctor, I am yours to the lowest pit of hell ; on which Barrow turned on his heel and said," And there, my lord, I leave you."— Old and New London.

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

The Duchess of Fife is still unwell. She and her husband will probably leave for tl.e South of France in the course of a few days for a prolonged stay at Cannes or Nice, which will take them well into the new year.

The remarkable weather that has prevailed since the beginning of September has resulted, in Kent, in second crops of pears and strawberries. Some of the latter are as large as hazel nuts, and almost fully ripe, while the " aftermath " of pears vary from an inch and a half to two inches in length.

Twenty-five thousand hungry children were fed last winter out of the funds accruing from a series of three dances given at Kensington. The destitute little diners were far away in the East-end of the parish of St. Augustine, Victoria-park. This is one of the practical and philanthropic ways of bringing togetber the East and the West.

An extraordinary amount of judicial patronage has fallen to the present Government. Another judgeship is now vacant in Scotland through the death of Lord Lee, one of the judges of the Scotch Division of the Court of Session. He died on Satur- day afternoon, at his residence in Edinburgh, after ten days' illness caused by a chill.

There is to be another :debate on the eight hours question. The case for the eight hours bills is to be stated by that most brilliant of Socialists. Mr. Geo. Bernard Shaw, and the case against will be stated by that excellent specimen of the old Radical school, and extremely vigorous public debater, Mr. G. W. Foote. It is to be hoped that St. James's Hall will be retained for the occasion, though as arrangements stand the scene will be the Hall of Science.

The rage for cheapness permeates almost every- thing, and has now reached suicide. Suicide on economical principles was indulged in the other night. Not wishing wastefully to pay for a re- volver which would only be used once, a man entered a shop and asked to be shown Due, using it there and then without payment. That :shopkeeper will in future take care to show firearms and am- munition separately to customers, and take care the customer doesn't get hold of both at once.

Felix Volkhovsky is the latest Russian refugee who has come to reside in London. He lives with Stepniak in a quiet street in St. John's-wood. He intends to devote himself henceforth to the cause of Russian freedom. Mr. Volkhovsky knows what it is to be in the grasp of the Russian police. Seven years of his life have been spent in solitary confine- ment and eleven years in exile in Siberia. He was sentenced for life, but managed to elude the vigil- ance of the Siberian police, and escaped. Ile spent about six months inCanada.

The difficulties of enforcing the new American tariff law have already commenced. It will entail no end of disputes, and the cost of levying the duty must be enormous; but as the tariff is imposed, not for purposes of revenue, but in the interests of manufacturers, the Government does not reckon the cost. It will help to reduce the surplus. The Act is full of elaborate and complicating details. There is a diversified schedule for every article ac- cording to the quality, as in the case of wool ; or according to dimensions, as the thickness of thread or width of cloth.

Since Lord Rosslyn's death we have seen no allu- sion to the well-known manner in which he received his appointment as Lord High Commissianer to the Church of Scotland. His services to his party, and his undoubted abilities, made it im- possible to pass him over. " What can we do with Rosslyn ?" said Dizzy, " Make him Master of the Buckhounds, as his father was," suggested one of his colleagues. "No," said the Premier, "he swears far too much for that; we will makehim High Com- missioner to the Church of Scoti=d l" And an excellent commissioner he made.

A Vienna evening paper publisltes a telegram I from St. Petersburg, according to which Dr.l Koucharsky, a young professor of medicine, com— mitted suicide in the presence of his class of stu- dents. He had just ended a lecture an acids, when he poured some drops frem the phial into a glass., "Attention, young men!" he said, "-in two minutes, you will see a man die. Good bye to you all I" He drank the liquid, drew out his watch, and counted the seconds until he fell to the ground a corpse:. The students were speechless and motionless: when they at last tried to apply antidotes A was too late_ Professor lioucharsky was dead.

The unusual combination of sabolarly attain,- ment and commercial energy in the Liberal candi- date for Eeeles was charmingly Mustrated a feNw weeks ago. The headmaster of the Manchester Grammar School was taken ill rather suddenly, and Mr. Roby was consulted about what should be dome to fill his place. The difficulty was speedily sur- mounted, Mr. Roby volunteering to do the wait himself. For nearly a month he kept at it. "It was delightful," he said to the friend who told the "Star man the incident, 'to leave the yarns and get away from the warehouse, and be amongst the boys for a while." It isn't every Lancashire cot-Jona spinner that could go and do likewise.

Professor Thorold Rogers was well known to monopolise a fgood deal of comversaton after din— ner. He was once dining at St. John's Cobsge,. Cambridge, where he had been engaged in looking over some of the historical manuscripts, and after dinner, as is the wont of the College, the Fellows assembled to drink their wine in the Combination Room. Professor Rogers talked incessantly, and the whole table listened with interest and attention to his amusing stories, but no one could even "get , a word in edgeways." In walking across the Court to his rooms with a friend, when all was done, he remarked, "What capital company your fellows are; I never knew people who could sustain a conversa- tion better."

The proposed Irish Channel Tunnel is now so far advanced as an actual project that the Mayor of Belfast has convened a public meeting to consider the scheme. He has convened the meeting on an urgent requisition signed by about 70 representa- tive men of the North of Ireland, who state their belief that a tunnel to connect the Antrim coast with the coast of Wigtonshire, and thereby the railway system of Scotland and England with Bel- fast and the North of Ireland, would be a great public advantage, and would have immense and far- reaching beneficial results to the three kingdoms. Preliminary investigations have been made by Messrs. James Barton and John G. Barton in con- junction with Messrs. Hawkshaw and Hayter of London.

There is something exceedingly ludicrous in an archdeacon asking mankind to pity him because he only made £2,000 by writing a" Life of Christ" and £4,000 by writing a "Life of St. Paul." The only authentic " Lives "of Christ purport to have been written by the Evangelists, and they, far from getting a large sum of money for their task, seem to have suffered serious personal inconvenience. As literary work, the archdeacon's " Lives " are not better than the Lives of Voltaire and Rousseau by Mr. John Morley. If then, these excessive sums were paid for the former compilations, it is rather due to the illustrations and to the subject matter than to the treatment. At most, they are a mere rehash of old facts, except where the archdeacon draws upon his imagination. That his " Life of Christ" conveyed this impression, is shown by the well-known answer to the Cambridge Examiner. .4 We know little of the childhood of Christ; what knowledge we hav we derive from Archdeacon 6 Farrar." It may, thereiOre, be said of these two books, "what is new is not true, Lind what is true is not new."

The Duke of Argyll is a witness to the truth of what he calls clairvoyance, though our contempor- ary "The Spectator," to whom his letter is addressed, prefers to describe it as " thought reading." Having been a spectator of a rather striking experiment in this way nearly forty years ago, the Duke of Argyll determined to "have grounds more relative than this," and thereupon. without giving a hint of his intention to any other person, he thought of a special room in a friend's house in England which was " very peculiarly and almost fantastically furnished," imagining it in his own mind with the distinctness which we are able to give to the stores of recent memory. The result, it is confessed, " as- tounded "him. "The clairvoyant (continues the narrative) described the room, with all its special and unique features, as if she saw it, but saw it with difficulty, through some darkness which it required some groping to penetrate. Not a word was spoken by me. She made out her vision with extraordinary truth." In conclusion, the Duke declares his con- viction that the power, as defined and limited in his statement, "was, however incomprehensible, a real power."
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1890.

Oxford University is becoming less Conservative. Mr. A. S. Peake, a Methodist and the son of a Methodist minister, Las been elected to a theological fellowship at Merton College. This, it is said, is the first time that either of our great universities has gone outside orthodox Anglicanism. Mr. Peake holds the Hebrew lectureship at Mansfield Collge, and is an eminent theological scholar.

A hypodermic blush is the latest variety of that occasionally pleasing article. It is obtained by in- serting colouring matter beneath the skin with the point of a syringe. The effect is described as mar- vellous. The blush lasts two hours. The owner of it

is indescribably beautiful for that period. Aft6r- wards she becomes of a greenish yellow complexion, and cannot wear her blush too often, because the syringe marks the skin with an ugly little scar. May that blush never be imported into England. It was born in America.
No woman of modern times has been honoured

with such an imposing funeral as that of Mrs. Booth. It must have been a trying moment for the General and his family, when, towards the close of the service, they rose, and grouping themselves about the coffin, sang the hymn which they had sung around Mrs. Booth's deathbed, "I shall pass through the valley of the shadow of death." Dur- ing the service the General and his daughters broke down more than once. The form of mourning worn by the daughters was a wide white scarf passing from the right shoulder and tying at the left side. Mr. and Mrs. Booth-Tucker, the Commissioners for India, wore white Indian draperies about their heads. The three little daughters of Mr. and Mrs. Bramwell Booth wore cream-coloured frocks and Salvation Army bonnets, with white scarves across their dresses.

The introduction of smol-eless powder into the battles of the future, necessitates among other al- terations a change of colour in the uniforms of our soldiers. For if they marched into the field under the approaching condition of things, their scarlet coats would afford the best possible targets to the rifles of the enemy. Scarlet is a colour which retains its hold on the vision when most of the other hues have lost their distinctive character. Hence, given a clear battlefield, to array the common soldier in his present accoutrements, is practically to clothe him in the garb of death. A conference has recently been held at headquarters to consider the question of wherewithal shall Tommy be clothed? The result of its deliberations has not yet taken practical shape, but it is possible a red-brick colour, or a reddish grey. known in the army as the Elcho grey,which stand very high on the list for los- ing their tints at short distances, will supersede the lethal scarlet.

THE HANDSOME MALE HOUSEKEEPER Hewes a rarity in our Mansion. We were used to flousy and blear-eyed housekeeper,. with slouch- ing shoulders and ambiguous knees. But here was a man that even the male residents agreed with a painful unanimity,was well set up and good-looking. Ile was just upon six feet in height, and made the most of his six feet. Mit his frame was so muscular and well-proportioned that he did not appear very tall. He was fair of complexion; fair also as to the abundant hair and moustache. His face was cer- tainly handsome, and that despite the facts that his eyebrows, much lighter in colour than his hair,met, and that his lower law projected slightly beyond the upper. Everyone in the Mansions fell in love-with him, after the different fashions of their age,.their sex and their callings. The children of the- musica couple on' the top-foor played games with him. The young men were rather proud to be seen drink- ing with hiin at the Radnor Arms or Host's. The officials of the Portuguese Naval COMMi93%OO gave him of the priceless. Havana cigars with whose aroma they made the first floor fragrant. Mr. and Mrs. Patterson both gossipped with him Ett every available opportunity.. Miss Esmond, the artist, begged the favour of a sitting, in his own room and the presence of his wife. The wife was a somewhat meagre womai,. with faded 'shreds of beauty in her white fin*. She rarely spoke and seemedloverwhel me d,almost.cowed, by the husband's physical superiority. But he made the deepest impression upon Mrs. Wardell. and not quite young widow on the same floor as the rooms of the-housekeeper. Perhaps this was because she was the most impressionable-person in the Mansion.. All the nameless an innumerable little nothings possible on behalf of a tonans,a woman,and awidow were done and made, after the fashion of nothings, a very considensble sum of something— at alllevents, in the embittered opinion of the two old maids, the Misses Ward, and of the female sweepers' and cleaners. Andiyet it was all done with such delicacy and good breeding that these opinions had no further expression than much head shaking. One evening;, when the handsome housekeeper had been with, us nearly a year, the white-faced , wife suddenly-ran out from their sitting-room, ker :face whiter then-ever,. her whole frame quivering. Shew flew along the passage to Mrs. Wardell'sroom and, without as much* as knocking, rushed 'in. "Oh, forgistamei" site gasped," but I Mnew you were in." 6` What is it asked the widow, catching the infection of her terror._ "I am terrified." "What at ?" "At him." "Your husband ?" "My husband ! Oh. yes." "But terrified of him? Surely, there must be some mistake. He is so refined, so gentlemanly." "He is so terrible. Hush! you don't hnow him as I do. I've been wanting to warn you a long time."
"Warn ine !" "Oh, yes, yes, yes, I know everthingt Don't think me harsh or even angry. I have, indeed, no cause to be."

"Certainly not. And therefore why warn me ?" "You don't understand me. I have no cause to be angry. Ent—forgive me—l am not so blind as the rest of the people here. And I fie awake for nights." "Hush He may be listening to, vs now. He is capable of, he is clever enough for, anything. Now, listen." She bent her white face close to Mrs. Wardell's strangely red one. "As you value your peace of %Ind in this world —as you value your soul in the next—have nothing to do with him.' "What do you mean?" "1)0 you know why Iran in here just now? For my life. He will kill me one of thee days. And I shall not be the first. Do you understand now what my warning means ?" There was a gentle knock at the door. Mrs. Wardell started as one starts at a familiar sound that has for the first time a new significance. "Come in !" she said, with a strange hoarseness in her voice. He entered. "Ah ! I thought my wife might be here. There is a gentleman, my dear, anxious to see the vacant rooms on this floor. It is late; but for the sake of our employer, I think —" The gentleman, as a matter of fact,was even then, in rather unmannerly fashion,looking into Mrs. War- dell's room. Not staring; only looking in a quiet, observant way, in keeping with his quiet, profes- sional manner. The woman rose, and went through her duty. The new-comer asked many questions • more about the people in the Mansions and herself, than about the rooms. But she had gone back to her old taci- turn mood. When the quiet professional gentleman called, as he had arranged, at ten the next morning, he found the Mansions unusually perturbed. The house- keeper's wife had died in the night, they said. The professional gentleman went straight to the house- keeper's room. He was followed by another man, built on much the same lines as himself, only that be was taller and broader, "What do you want ?" asked the housekeeper, blocking up his doorway. " We hear that your—wife is dead." "Yes. Are you &medical man ?" "I am a professional man, and I arrest you Claude Llewellyn." The taller and broader man had slipped the hancuffs on with admirable dexterity. " For murder," the other went on imperturbably. " It's not murder," he shouted, conscious of Mrs. Wardell's face at the back of his captors. "This may not be, Tom," said the professioal gentleman, removing the housekeeper's wig and revealing a close-cropped black head.' My warrant is for one of the others." "I tell you," he blustered, "my wife died of heart- disease of long standing." "And I tell you," said the professional gentleman, " she was your mother, not your wife : and if she died of heart-disease, it was of a brokenheart. Come along Tom, the game's up."—The Home Provider.

div.head: NEW BISHOP OF ROCHESTER:
div.p: THE NEW BISHOP OF ROCHESTER:

The Queen has been pleased to approve of the nomina- tion of the Very Rev. Randal Thomas Davidson, D.D., Dean of Windsor, to succeed the Bishop of Rochester on his translation to the see of Winchester. Dean Davidson was born in 1848, and educated at Harrow and at Trinity College, Oxford, where he graduated B.A. in 1871, and M. A. i n 1875. In May,lBB3,he was appointed by the Queen to the delnery of Windsor, and also resident chaplain in ordinary to her Majesty. He also holds the following appointments : Registrar of the Order of the Garter, Commissary for the Bishop of Adelaide, and Trustee of the British Museum.

div.head: SOCIALIST CONGRESS.
div.p: THE SOCIALIST CONGRESS.

CALMS, TUESDAT.—At to-day's sitting of the Socialist Congress 2,800 persons were present. Dr. Aveling delivered a speech, in the course of which he declared that his presence as a British delegate was an affirmation of the international principle and the solidarity of work- ing men. When he returned among his comrades in England he would tell them that Calais with its factories closely resembled a city of the dead, which was a sign that the social revolution was putting an end to the miseries of his brethren. At the close of the sitting an order of the day was passed unanimously, declaring that the inhabitants send an expression of sympathy and Socialist sentiments to the British workmen who have given proofs of their solidarity, and also to the workers assembled at Hall.

SACRED% CONCERT AT WARRINGTON. INFIRMARY BENEFIT. The sacred concert which was given in the Public Hall on Sunday evening "by the Warrington Glee and Mairigal Union,. assisted by an orchestra, in aid of the Infirmary new extension,was a great success in every, respect. The attendance was large,the hall being crowded in alltparts, while- the vocalists and orchestra acqnittedtthemselves in a manner which won the unstinted praise of an who heard them. The follbwing are the names of the artistes and orchestra—artistes: soprani, Mesdames P. Walsh, G. Woods, Dobson, Misses Cavanagh, Hedgcockl and Jones;. contralti,. Mrs. Hodges,, Misses Fanshawe, Andrew, and Eckersley ;. tenon, Messrs. W. S. Howard, W. Fryer, J. W. Whittle, and Joseph Bate; bush. Messrs. R.Bccles, Charles McDowell, D. Fan- shawe,. and J. The con- ductor and promoter of the concert was Mr. George Woods. The concert opened with an im- pressive rendering of the late Cardinal Newman's beautiful hymn, "Lead, kindly Light," the audi- ence :joining with the choir. The subsequent pro- gramme was, as will be seen, admirably arranged, being as follows :—Solo and chorus, As pants tke hart," (Crucifixion), solos NtisaCtara Hedgcock ; recitation and aria, "In native worth," (Creation), solo, Mr. W. S. Howard, aria, "0 rest in the Lord," (Elijah), Miss Fanshawe; solo and chorus, "To Thee, great Lord," (Moses in Egypt), soli, Miss Cavanagh, Messrs. Fryer. and Fanshawe; recitation and aria, "With verdure clad,' (Creation), Mrs. Dobson ; chorus," Splendentete, Deus,"' (Motett), soli, Misses Cavanagl: and Fanshawe, and Messrs. Fryer and Eccles ; duet and chorus, "I waited for the Lord," (Hymn of Praise) soli ; Mrs. P. Walsh: and Miss Andrew: song. "Calvary," Miss Cavanagh.;: solo and chorus, "Hear my prayer," solo, Mrs. Dobsan ;- song, "The lost chord," Mrs. P. Walsh; song, "The good shepherd." It is no exaggeration to say that this long and by no, means easy programme was rendered with the greatest precision and success. There was no hitch throughout., and nothing in the slightest degree to mar the complete enjoyment of the audience. Both the band and the choir deservedly won the golden opinions of those present, and with regard to the soloists it would be invidious to dis- criminate between those who in their various pasts, did equally well. The appreciation of the audience was frequently attested by applause which could not alto- gether be suppressed by the consideration thab the con- cert was held on a Sunday evening. , Mr. George Woods was a most efficient conductor, and to, him the signal success of a gathering, the result of his untiriiig energy, must have been extremely gratifying. it is very satisfactory to be able to add that as a. result of the concert the sum of over £2O will be added to the funds of the Infirmary.

the library, whole her Masud 104 cl her imra° diately,„._ • - • • ft We need not follear them thither. We will not intrude upon that re-union. There was much to tell, and the clock had struck twelve before anyone ventured to knock at the door of the library. But Edward lost no time. As soon as he per- ceived that the General and his father, with the remainder of the household, were deeply engaged in speculation and reminiscence, then he hurried out to the stables, and, saddling his mare, rode quickly through the village. As he passed through it he nearly ran over a man. "Curse you, stupid head!" said the fellow "can't you look where you are going to ? " "I know that voice," muttered Edward. "Come, I didn't hurt you," he said, aloud; you needn't be so savage, "Sandy" Sam!" "Who are you that knows me in the dark. If ye have such good eyes, I wonder ye didert see me on the road." "I am in a hurry. But, I say Sam, I wouldn't adviseyou to rernainlong about here ; the governor has his eye upon you. A nod is as good as a wink, eh?" "Thankye, Master Edard; now I know ye. ni take your advice. Ecl a been away long ago, only I hadn't the 'ready.' I was cruel ill-used." "Here's five shillings for you; and now- tell me, have you seen Minnie Layton this evening?" " What—me ? How should I see the girl?' Who I told ye I had?" (Oh, Sam, Sam, you are a very small villain, after all. Conscience betrays vou at once!) Edward Watson was immediately struck with the tone and manner of the reply, and, catching the man by the collar, he said: Look here, Sam—no nonsense. When did yonsee Minnie Layton last? Tell the truth, and I'll give you ten pounds down to-night'.. Tell me a falsehood, and I'll get you a month with, hard labour very seem. I know something too!" "Ye wouldn't be so hard, Master Ed'ard. Yet wouldn't crush a pore woundedworm like me." "Yea I would, replied Edward. "Some worms' ought to be killed. Now the truth, or, by heaven, I'll put the constabulary upon you to-morrow." "You'll swear you'll never tell / told you." "I will—l do. Go on." "Well then, young Marmadule Deane ho tried to take her away. I was in the job too. He drove her insensible to Bishop's Creek, and there put her into a boat—' Edward gave vent to a wish concerning Marma. duke's-. future welfare which shall not be set down here. "Sandy ''" Sam proceeded— "He put her into the boat, but he left her for a minute to fasten up the horse. She got up and pulled away in the *boat out to sea, and there she is." "Thank God. lehe is at any rate safer than in Deane'S power.. "Sandy" Sam, I'm your. debtor. The money shall be yours. Can you pull an ear " Yes, sir, a,little bit," 'Gems on, then; catch' my PAlle.. There's another ten pounds waiting for you at home. Now run along at your best pace." Edward started, and "Sandy" Sam feeling really honest for once„kent pace manfully. Before long the pair had strived at the creek. Here "Sandy" quieldy found a, punt, into which he and Edward stepped, and pulled away in the direction they fancied Minnie had gone.. After a while they lay on their oars, and listened for any sound or signal that might intimate where Minnie was drifting. But le/I a long time nothing could be diatinguished but the restless "lapping" of the ripples against the sides of the boat. "What became ot that brute i" inquire/ Edward

at That. "Which? Mr. Marmaduke I" inquired "Sandy" Sam, "or your horse?" "Of course I meant Deane; but I wonder what has become of her—the mare, I mean.' "He put out in, nt skill after Miss Minnie," said. "Sandy." "But hell never find her in the dark. He can't pull as well as she can." " Listen ; didn't t you hear something'll.' said Edward, suddenly. "Hush! surely I heard the plash of oars. Pull, you." The boat's head, was turned, and after a few powerful strokes the men sat still and: again listened. Nothing could be hoard. Edward then went forward into the bow' of the boat, and after whispering to" Sandy" Ram to scull very gently, and with as little noise as possible, he sat on the watch, leaning over, almost touching the water. At length he caught sight of a dark object a little to the right of "Pull your right," he said to his companion, and the boat's head turned in the required direction, ypt they seemed notto gain much upon it. Go on, Sam, full speed; we must catch, her up. Ilbrhaps it is 'Minnie," "Perhaps it's the other one,' muttered "-Sandy' Sam. "If it is, I shall catch it nicely. I hope'he'll kilt him 1." Edward Watson did not utter a word as the 'boat sped onwards. It was rapidly overtaking the float- ing object now. In a few minutes it would be alongside. He was in a fever of expectation,. Three minutes more anclithe boats were alongside each

other. Seated, pulling wearily a pair of heavy seulls,was Minnie Layton. Lying at the end of the boati, in a "huddled up" condition, dripping with sea water, and apparently insensible, was a figure of a man. "Minnie, my darling Minnie," exclaimed Edward Watson, as he sprang into the boat and claspod hex in his arms. "Are you safe and well? " "Quite well, disar," she replied, returning. his caress. "But look at him! Is he dead P" She pointed to the heap at the end of the boat, and Watson stepped across the thwarts, , turned the body over, and found it was Marmaduke Deane himself. " How came:this scoundrel here? Get up I Come, rouse yourself, you pitiful cowardT' He saluted Marmaduke with a kick as .he spoke, and felt almost:inclined to throw him into the Bea. "I can't get rip. I'm half frozen here in my wet clothes," replied the recumbent youth, , now corn. pletoly cowed..:. "Miss Layton has forgiven .me, and you may as well. lam quite ready to make any amends. Let me be." "How did,l he come in here r''askel Edward, turning to Minnie again. "He had 'come up with me in • anotherrboat, and offered to take me back. Ile was apparently sincere, but I wouldn't trust him," replied, Minnie. "I pulled away; and somehow be stood up in his own skiff and fell over. I helped to pull Aim out, fox he can't swim much, and then I triedlto reach the shore. is was pulling away from it. when I heard you "What asplen did girlyou are,l"' exclaimed Edward; admiringly_ "Fancy you, saving that cur's Hs after all I think I shouldlave let him drown." "'Vengeance is Mine,'" quoted Minnie "and he was so Aelplees. Besides,. I am net afraid of him now.P believe he is quite ashameci:af himself, and very penitent." "Sc he ought to be.. Here,, Sam. Take out your young master, and pull him ashore. We don't: wantliim in this boat."' Bak before Sam could execute this order. Marmas. duke eot up, and said,: "VII save him the trouble, Watson, I can. apologise to you move readily than I can to Miss, Minnie. I have behaved like a,thorough scoundrel. I confess. But I ,ffill reform, in future.' She has. taught me a lesson I shall never forget. I have only- onefavour to ask. Try to keep this evening's work quiet. I will secare Sam's silence," he continued ; "and as I am indeed really sorry—and I wish 1 could prove it—l will leave hero directly, an never trouble you agan. Miss Mamie, g did love. you very much. I net help it now. But I was carried away by passion and jealousy. Good-bye. Good- bye Watson. You will behappy. Farewell !:" There was, after all,, a kbut of dignity in the manner in which he bade his former friends good. bye. They returned us farewell, and gave him their bands in token of forgiveness, and in &minute ox two ho had, with "Sandy "' Sam, disappeared in the direction of the shore. Watson,. putting Minnie carefully Ira the stern sheets of the boat, sculled back to the creek. The mare was there, &cart was procured, and the animal was harnessed. In this tough and-ready convey- ance the young' people arrived at the '" Towers about midnight, where some startling news awaited them..

CHAPTER MI.. THOU ART THB MAN! Mae. Lenox was not at first much alarmed al Minnie's absence, but when evening set in and eight drew on, she became alarmed; and, putting on het bonnet, went out in search of her. She made in. quince at every place she thought it likely Minnie might have gone to, and at last she determined to gc to the "Towers," and see Edward Watson. It was a good walk, but the night, though dark was fine and celm. Mrs. Layton lost no time, anS it was scarcely nine o'clock when she artived and inquired for "Mr. Edward." "They are at dinner," replied the servant; "but come in, Mrs. Layton,'and I will say you are here." Luov came in, and in a few minutes a message came for her to go up into the library, where Mr Edward would see her. She went upstairs accord- ingly, and almost immediately Edward came hit, the room. "Good evening, Mrs. Layton. What can Ide for you? I cannot remain ,very long, as we have friends to dinner ?" "I came about Minnie," said the woman. "Minnie—what about her? Is anything eat matter ?" "Don't you know, then? She left home thret hours ago and more, and'l find she has taken a bundle. Didn't she see you ?" "No; I have not set eyes on her since yesterday,' replied Edward, fervently. "Are you certain sho has taken a bundle? Why did she leave so, sud- denly ?" "We had some words shout that young Deane," replied Mrs. Layton, "and she declared she'd marry no one else but you." "Darling!" murmured Edward. "And then a message came, and she went npstairs. I didn't take any notice, knowing her ways, until just at dusk ihappened to go up, and, not finding hers' searched. But she wasn't about. Then I missed one or two things of hers, and then I found. she had taken what things she could carry away. As satin as I discovered all this I went around and not finding her, came on here, supposing, to tell you the truth, that you bed a hand in the business. That's' the wholo affair," added Mrs. Layton, begin- ning to cry, "and I wish she wasn't so contrary." "We must find her immediately," said Edward. " seertwhat can be done." " Perhaps she's gone to the Hall," suggested Mrs. Layton:" "No, scarcely.. X cannot go now. We have friends dining here, I will ask them what to do. Meantime, I will see about getting the horses saddled. We must set off soon." Edward anturned tothe dining-room , and his absence was naturally remarked upon. The dessert was on the table. Ile was in a very unenviable position, for he must declare his attachment to Minnie, else his anxiety concerning her would be misconstrued, and he tronbled to think how his parents and his father's guests would receive the ietelligence. "Yes," replied Edward, "Minnie has left home and her mother wants help to and her." "Why should she come here then ?" asked Lady Watson. "Why inquire for you ?" !` Because Minnie and I have seen a good deal of each other latelY, and se I am an old friend—" "What" exclaimed Sir Walter angrily. "If don't knowthat; remarked Sir William Deane —" Marmaduke slid."' "Your son-? Dm you mean lit' toll me that this girl is fitted to:marry a gentleraan ? " cried Lady Watson-4 "As fares marater and appearance go," said the General, stoutly; "1 must say ;she would be only au orne-eent teensy household. Bat her station in life ; =Mar acccamllshments: are not what we ex- pect or desire for me son ! " "Certainly not," assented Sir Walter; "nor for mine either. Edward, you are asrass—an id;ot! Tell the woman to go-about her business. We can't be, answerable for-every railway brat." "Father," said'Edward, with dignity, and, rising': as he spoke, "L hope you won't think me disre- spectfelSbat I am attached to this young lady." "Young Itsit —Young beggar-!" exclaimed hiss father; anemilT. Goma, no nonsense, Edward.. , Sit down; den,telbisus have any tragedy airs, if yens please. Ring the bell, Lily?' "WhaHor may I inquire ?"said Lady Watson'. "I think it is MT lAMB to-9" ..7" Go to-Bath ! "'said Sir Walter, who had quite- lost his tempers at the unparalleled temerity of his, son. "Tee, I am," he asaswered, somewhat-taken aback. " To, whom else ? Who are you, indeed ?" "A most miserable woman," said Lucy,. raising her veil; wretched and unhappywomaso." She had scarcely lifted the veil front her face when General Deane uttered an exclamation which twined all evesttowards him. Well did he know the ham, 'though many years had passed: over it and changed its beauty.. The face was one never to be faaVatten, and' the General remembered it too well. Captain Tanshleigh was sitting- with his back to, the; d oor, andi had not turned his heads Sir William, continued:: "What'a-the matter, General; do you know this, person?" asked Sir Walter, the Bear. "I think I dm," replied tha General; "or I fancy- I did. Ibis many years amend yet-----" "Oh, well, if you know her she's all right. FVe, heard obout her, and her living with Collier." "That's not ;rue, Sir Walter Watson," said Lucy Layton, flushing angrily. "If you say that,, you repeat a lit."' Cap- tain Rushleig,h rose, and turning round, gazed at the angry lady for a moment; then, addressing his hest, he said firmly: "Held, Sir Walter! div.p: CHAPTER XXXTL TUE LAST OF ?HE STORY.

luttCY LAYTON had been seated with her restored husband for some time, until at last the long inter- view was ended. She had told him all. She had related her hopes and fears, her determination to " pay out" the General fox his interferences and had at length confessed how Nature had beaten her. She gave up the game, and had already determined to make a clean breast of the matter when the sudden discovery of her husband's identity precipi- tated events. The General, his wife, and Sir Walter and Lady Watson, with Lily, were in the drawing-room when Captain and Mrs. Layton, as we must call them, entered it. General Deane had had for the moment a struggle with himself. When he heard the distinguished officer Rushleigh rise and proclaim himself, as Frank

Layton, all tlie circumitartees of the siege of Delhi and many ether incidents came again before him. It was Layton, then, who had piloted him to the tamp, and who had afterwards saved his life. He fancied that Layton was ignorant of all the circum- stances preceding the court-martial, and the execu- tion. He had been in the ranks—he was now a distinguished officer. How could the General meet him, after all he had done, without fearing that Layton might in his turn betray him? For he had strong reasons, as we shall see, for this belief. There was nothing but coneuntuletion for husband and wife. Lady Deane forgot all animosity, and of all the party the only uncomfortable and gloomv ones were Captain Layton, alias Enshleigh, and Ins wife. great cloud weighed upon them both, and a terrible confession had to be made—a confession more humiiating than even Lucy Layton fancied, for she had been endeavouring to injure the man who had, at the risk of his professional reputation saved litr husband. Little by little Lucy told her story with shame- faced mien and tearful eyes. Amid the most profound' silence, she related all the events, and her only ev-' , cure -was the General's interference, and his deter.' mined condemnation of her husband to death. Then Layton himself rose, and painful as it was for him to read the flimsy veil of apology from his, wife, he did it manfully. He told them how lonel Deane had, in effect, saved his (Layton's) life. Ho had seen him in his cell, and, in a mea- sure, connived at his escape. He was aware of the exchange which the poor, ruined officer had made for the corporal, mad then Lucy Layton's sin and prospects of vengeance were piteously exposed. The' astonishment, and, we may add, the sincere satisfaction of Sir William and Lady Deane were unbounded when they learnt the relationship of Minnie and Marmaduke respectively; and when Ed- ward came in 'with the young lady, tired, pale, but safe, and clinging to him, he and Minnie were both astonished by the kisses and congratulations showered upon therm by all, even by Mrs. Layton., who was nevertheless terribly depressed. Sir Walter and Lady Watson were particularly pleased. The former was as fervent in his praises' of his son's acumen and choice of a wife as he had been in condemning him at dinner. He apologised to Mrs. Layton and the captain, and made things' worse. But at last things got themselves righted, and the Deanes carried,off Minnie in triumph to the' "I wonder what Marmaduke will say," said Sir- William as they reached home. But Marmaduke said nothing. He had gone to • bed, and long before breakfast next morning he had left the Hall. A note to Sir William explaining the circumstances frankly was found in his room. He was traced, however, by his real father and ' mother, and under thhir judicious treatment turned out welL Captain , Layton and his wife at once quitted the neighbourhood, and lived abroad for- mally years Intent upons,the education of Marina- duke,. who soon entered the Austrian army, and did well his profession' * *, * *-•

Edward and Minnie were married as soon as tho former had got employment. They, sailed for India some time ago to inspect the railways there for - Oovernment. Thus, after all, Sir Walter's and Sir William's pet project was carried out, and the pro- perties are united in their children. Miss Lily Watson. has now come out, and has attracted Some Attention. She is not yet 'married, but at the last State itazo she danced with a fine and handsome officer. of Austrian Hussars, who admires her immensely, and we may hope to hear of. a. wedding next year. ,ILucy Layton is noirquite happy with her husband,. find confesses that her ideas have undergone a change Rer the better since-she decided that." THE. TICINO REVOLUTION.

CITARGE AGAINST CASTIONI. Bow-street Police Court, London, was crowded on Saturday with Swiss and others intereated in the charge against Angelo Castioni of having murdered Councillor Rossi during the recent revolution in Ticino. Mr. Grain said that he intended at once to raise the question whether this was a political offence or not, and to put witnesses from Ticino in the box who would deny that the accused fired the shot which proved fatal to Rossi. The matter was a very serious one, and one into which he was in- structed to go into very fully. Castioni, who was not brought into court, was formally remanded until to-day (Saturday.)

TILE HAVEN OF HEALTH. Birmingham Sitturdcry In our issue of ~S'ataivlay Tiqht plarc;it Ist, I.B90) we, Vullished the thrilling story of how Thomas Durrant was literally snatched back from the grave. A narrative like that, teeming with interest, and better still bearing; truth's hall mark an every line, reminds us once more I that fact is stranger than faction. When Tom Durratit left the hospital he was dying, thedoctors said they hat 'done their best for him and could do no more. Of his illness, his terrible sufferings, we have speken ;before. Everything had failed; and there seemed; nothing for it but for a mother to bow iher head with tetalul resignation over the sictt bed, around which the shadows of the spirit-world appeared to I.)e rapid stealing. We 'have spoken of the tierce battle-which was waged with disease, ending in a.glorious victory for that tridy won- derful medicine known as Warner's " SAFE" Cure. Our representative called ion Thomas Durrant, 79, Camp-hill, Birmingham, the last week of Febtuary, a full account of the interviewnppearing in the i following issue of Saturday/fight. Wr, left the young man very weak and thin, but still able to get about withthe aid of

a stick. Owing to business and other reasons, we did not call again until Monday last, ,Itme 9, when late:- in the after- noon we were once more urhered into the ccsy sitting- room of 79, Camp-hill, by Mrs. Durrant. " Here he is. Tom, you remember this gentleman, • don't you ? " Thus spoke the mother as yecang Durrant entered the room. We eh ook hands, and during the pre- liminary greetings we kook the opportunity of closely scrutinising the invalid. He had altered greatly sincelast we had seen him. Dining our first interview (February) he had been wrapped -up in shawls, usecta stick in walk ing, across the room,and seemed almost too.weak to stand up straight. On Monday he walked into the room as straight as a dart and without a stick, sem dispensing with the shawls he hail worn at our last meeting. In answer to our inquiry as to how he was getting • along, he said, "Famously, thanks. 'Nes, I look very different to •iiihat I did when you were bee last. Then, if you remember, I had not been allowed to go out ; but I passed that stage by some time, and new get out for a walk in the bright, warm sunshine eveas. day when the weather will permit. " All the signs of dropsy have goneand all that I have left of the paralysis Is a slight stiffness in the left leg and fingers. 'have a splendid appetite, and can feel myself : getting stronger every day. I am Mt only alive, for which alone I might well feel thahkful, but I am alive and promising tolive many more yearmyet. And all this • simply from one cause. I feel a lump mis_ng in my throat as I think of it. I should have been lying in my gravel months ago but fir Warner's SAFE' Cure." This, gentle rer, der, is a plain, simple, unvarnished narrative of hovel'homas Durrant was "Brought back from the grave." The facts as told hero can be proved to the entire satitfaction of all who are suffering them- selves, or who have any near and dear one suffering from perhaps the most fatal disease knovrntc modern science. There is no ptiff about this; this is no newspaper Bain, Thomas Durrant is) known to each member of the staff bf this paper. (His recovery has been a subject of congratu- lation and, marvellous though the,recovery has been, one and all of us can easily and gladly testify to the truth of this narrative.
'THE ALLEGED A TTRMYMO MURDER AT WARRINGTON. 'EXTRAORDINARY AFFLIR.

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Tuesday, Thomas bolt, employed as a puddler at Messrs. Monks Hall ,and Co's. Works, Bank Quay, was • charged on remand with having unlawfully and with malice ,aforethought attempted to murclar Mary Lyons, a woman aged 41, by ;throwing tier into the Ilivar Mersey, at Hawley, ar. Monday, the

20th September. Before the case was proceeded with the magistrate, Mr. W. H. Bleekley, referred tothe remarks made by Mr. S. Rigby laseweek as to the right of eeporters to he present duringthe hearing of the case. Ile (Mr. Blecklee-) wished it to be distinctly understood by the gentlemen of , - the press, tlaatia a Court of that kindthe magistrates, - if they chose, could keep the reporters and the public • out entirely. But he did not think there was any neces- sity for excluding them from the hearing then of the • case before then., and it would, therefore, be heard in • the presence of reporters. The Clerk (Mr. Buckton), addressing the :reporters "kit . as a matter of fact you have no right to beptesent in Cak./3 • of this kind: -it is entirely in the discretion of the magistrates whether they admit you OT not. There seems to be a mistake about this, and it it better you - should understand the facts. Sergeant Barnes said he was instructed the Inspec- tor to apply for a further remand for eight days in order that the police rMght make more enquiries respecting ' the case. John Shakeshaft, porter in the warehouseAof the Ship • Canal Co., and residing at Gaskell-St., said between one and two o'clock on the day in question, he -was walking . along the Cheshire side of the river Mersey, a.nd on the ' Lancashire side of the river he saw a man . and woman lying on the grass. Shortly afterwards he saw the woman get up. and she walked ;about a,hundred yards in the direction al 'Warrington. Before the woman • stopped the man stood up and shouted to her that • she had robbed him, and he then.,proceeded towards her. A quarrel ensued, during which the man said: " If you don't turn the money up, I'll throw you in the river," which threat he repeated several times and the • prisoner then took held of the womarea arm and pulled her towards the river; but she fell on her knees and shouted muz der. Prisoner remained.elose to the woman ',whilst she was in this, position for about five minutes, and afterwards snatched a bundle from her, and threw it into the water, and again threatened the woman that '-he would do the same with her. Carrying out his threat he took hold of the woman and rolled her into the water. The distance from the top of the boa*, to the surface•of the,water would be four or five feet. Jae soon as witness .discovered the woman seas in the water lie shouted to the workmen who were employed at the Howley Tannery, ..ancealso requested the prisoner to get the woman mitt • but the latter replied that he could not reach her and walked away towards Warrington. The prisoner resembled the man whom witness saw with, the woman, but he rendered no assistance whatever towards saving her from drowning. Some-men from the Tannery, in _answer to his calling, procured a fire-rake and were suc- ,cessint in safely dragging the woman out of the water, -though in a aery fatigued condition, for she had gone under:the water twice. The prisoner. was .arrested near -the tannery by some other men. Flenrffoster, fireman, emeloved at Howley tannery, .said that et the time named he saw the prisoner and the ;woman in a field near the river,•which was ,on the same ,side of the river as was the tannery- They Appeared to be quarrelling; but witness could riot hear what it was 'about. Fin,noticed the accused get hold of the woman's -arm and mill her to the side ofahe river and he saw ;her fall. Prisoner then rolled her down the lealik'into the 'water. Witness at once procured e. fire rake, which was about ten feet lone and proceeded-to the river with it. It was, however, taken from him by a man named 'Cummings who held it to the unfortunate person,,kelpless in the water. Happily she had strength to grasp at, and Cannmines was successful in draggingher to the side,and With the megistance of a man ruunedjoseph Jollsy, he -ultimately got-her on the bank. Witness saw the peieoner -walking ,quietly away, and afterwardseibseevedthat he vas stopped and detained by some Men. John Cummings, tanner's labourer, livikig at Tilley-et„ gave evidence in corroboration of the statement made by the last witness with respect to his dragging the woman tram the ,water ; after which Constable Dean stated that in consequence of infornsre tion he received-he went to Howley, at the time and ,day in question. vehente saw the prisoner was bathe custody of men; and also the woman who gave her name as Mary Lyons. 'rhe woman was saturated from head to foot with water, and she was very much exhansted. The ; woman was then taken up to the prisoner, who told her that she had robbed him of 2s. 9d. ; but this charge she denied. The man repeated the charge to which the woman said" you threw me into the river." Witness , then took both persons into custody. On the way to the police station the prisoner said the woman had no right to rob him of the money, and witness replied, "You had no right to throw her into the river; you should have reported the theft to the police." The pri- soner then said, "If she had turned the money up I should not have thrown her into the river. I did in the heat of passion." At the station witness charged the prisoner with attempting to murder the woman by throwing her into the river Mersey at Howley Quay, in , reply to which prisoner said," I don't disown it." The woman was then taken to the parade room; stripped of her wet clothes ; had rugs put round her and placed near 'the fire. She afterwarde vomited a great deal, and was 'taken to the Workhouse in a cab, with a warning that She would be required the following morning at the pelice station. She did not, however, arrive the subse- quent day, and witness believed she had left the town; for she had not since been seen ; though vigorously -searched for. Mr. C. N. Spinks, medical officer at the Warrington 'W,orkbouse, deposed that at eight o'clock on the evening Of the 29th ult.. he was sent for to see the woman at the Workhouse. He found her in one of the wards in bed attended by a nurse. She had complained to the nurse that her shoulder was dislocated; but on examination he found it was not fractured or dislocated at-all. Witness ordered her some warm tea, and promised to see her in the morning. She required no treatment, aid seemed comfortable and fairly well. When witness went to visit her the succeeding morning she had gone. Sergeant Barnes, stationed at Padgate, deposed to receiving the prisoner into custody on the 30th Septem- ber, and charging him with the attempted murder, to which prisoner replied "I did it in the heat of passion, I would it had not have happened for the world." The Place where the occurrence took place was in the town- ship of Poulton. Prisoner had been twice remanded since his apprehension to enable him (Sergeant Barnes) to find the woman, but in this he had failed. In answer to the Clerk the prisoner said he had nothing to say, and he was sorry the affair had happened. The prisoner was then committed to take bis trial At he next Assizes held in thdcoMAY,

His premptxess was very creditable, bat he (Mr. Husband) was sorry his endeavours did not save the girl's life.—Annie McGowan, mat:en at the Infirmary, deposed that the deceased was admitted into the Institution shortly after eleven on Saturday morning stiffering from burns about the thighs atidabdomen. Deceased was attended by Dr. Smith, but expired about four -o'clock the succeeding day —The Deputy-Coroner remarked that cases of (shad burning were still very frequent; but he thought the present ease did not require any remarks from him. At the same titre he would likethildren, when left in a house by their parents to wear clothes which would pet catch fire se soon.—The jury returned a verdict of " AccidedUil Death."

Thornton announced that all -contributions received in the offertory box at the door would be devoted to the building of a new chapel. On Monday a tea meeting was held, at which there was a large attendanee. The tea was prepared and the tables presided over ley the ladies of the church in a manner which contributed materially to the success of the gathering. Anentertainment was afterwards given by several members a the church andchildren of the school, the chair being occupied by Mr. G. Sambrook. The proceedings were diversified by a fruit banquet, and brought to a fitting close by a sale by auction of the fruit and other s.milar offerings. the whole proceeds being devoted to the fund for the building of a new chapel.

PADGATE. Theannual harvest festival was held at Padgate Chureh on Sunday. The church, which had been most tastefully decorate( Flay Mrs. Langham and a staff of some twenty workers, looked extremely pretty. The ser- vices throughout the day were bright and hearty. There was a celebration of the Efoly Communion at eight o'clock At 10:30 the church,was well filled with parishioners, to most of whom the harvest is a matter of personal con- cern. The sermon was preached by the Rev. T. Rigby, vicar of St. Peter's, Warrington, who based his dis- course on Ruth ii. 7. The anthem was taken from Psalm cxvii., "0 praise the Lord." In the eveuing the church was crowded to overflowing, many people being unable to gain admission. The olsoir entered by the vestry door singing the processional hymn 382. "Come, ye thankful people, come." There were special psalms and lessons, and the anthem " lie watereth the hills " (Psalm civ.; 13) was well rendered by the choir. The sermon was preached by the Vicar (the Rev. J. J. Longhorn) from Hosea viii. 7. The offertories, which amounted to over £l3, will be applied to the support of the Padgate and Woolston Schools.

STRETTON. On Sunday the annual services of thanksgiving for the safe ingathering of the harvest were held in Stretton Church, which wag tastefully decorated. The Chancel screen was the work of Mrs. Dodd, wife of the Vicar, the pulpit and font were embellished by Mrs. Charles Whitley, the eagle by Mrs. Ellison, the gasaliers by Miss Lowe, the pillars by Mr. Joseph Hargreaves (head gar defier at Appleton Hall), assisted by Mr. John Cooper, and the alter rails, east end of the church by Miss Dodd. Several services were held during the day. At half-past eight o'clock there was a celebration of the Holy Com- munion, followed by morning service at half-past ten, and on this occasion the preacher was the Vicar (the Rev. Canon Dodd), who discoursed upoa the words "He hath given thee a law which shall not be broken." In the afternoon the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. F. Timins, one of the curates of St. Elphin's Warrinton, and in the evening by the Rev. Wilfrid Richmond, vicar of Birtles and Diocesan InsiSector of Schools. There were large congregations, especially that which assembled in the evening. Appropriate harvest hymns were sung, and the solos in the anthem, were taken by Messrs. Thomas Ditchfleld, Charles Potts, James Bury, and John Win- stanley. Mr. John Ellison was at the organ. The offerorties amounted to £l4.

IMPRISONING HIS GAOLERS. Lawrence Mooney, a cabdriver, has escaped from Limerick prison. Ile was confined on remand, charged with stealing money `from a Rathdrum tradesman, but was liberated from his cell and ordered to sweep the hall Observing the key of the outer door projecting from the lock, he sauntered to the prison entrance, closed the door, locked it from the outside, and disappeared, leaving his gaolers imprisoned. The officials, "locked up," were unable tintil nearly an hour had elapsed to communicate with the police; and though many officers, some mounted, were then sent in pursuit of Mooney, he has not been captured yet.

div.head: TURNER MAWINGS AT TICE ART GALLERY.
div.p: TURNER MAWINGS AT TICE ART GALLERY.

There is at present on view in the 'Warrington Art Gallery a .collection of drawings and eketches of the highest valuennd interest. The collettion consists! of no fewer than sixty-five drawings in pencil and water-colours by Turner, and jams' been lent to thi local Art Gallery for a period of 'twelve months by, the Trustees of the National 'Gallery. The Com-' mittee arete be congratulated on the acquisition,! and the curator, Mr. C. Madeley, upon the goodly, show whiCh he has made. *The drawings are: especially interesting and valuable—particularly: to students—from the facttlitit they illustrate the great artist's methods of work. Tbare are amongst, them, -pencil sketches in 'merest outline as well; as higlity-finished coloured pictures, and, in: one ingtance, there is a 'captivating study partly in 'penoilled outline !and pertly finished sin • colours. The collection !is 'hung at the farther and of the Art Gallery, and even a cursory 'glance will assure 'the 'lover of art that trz sees- anti knows Turner in these drawings 'better even 'than he does in some 'Of his larger vvetks !of world-wide repute. Most ofthe drawingsrsveal ! the most painstakingcare inlinishing the minutest details, a thing which ought to'be borne inn:tit-id by 'those who are sometimes too 'ready to suggest,that Turner painted anything any way and allowed it to pass for genius. 'ln this •class should be men- -tinned a pencil sketch of 'ront Hill (number :-E74). an architectural drawing (C7B). five studies of 'Bruges, Lausanne, '&c.' a Norman Tower, and, above all, a wondeffully finiShed picture !(M). of a 'Highland river scene. ThiS test-named pencil 'draw- in-g must be pronounced perfect of its kind, the delicacy of outline and -faultless perspective, and • the repose which, as a summer scene, rests-A:Ton it ill are such as -only a; man skilful as a draughts- man, and with genius to !boot, could possibly pro- duce. Two drawings of shipping (575 and 72) are quite contrastsin their way. One shows a:free and bold treatment !of Dover With a Dutch-built ship is the foregroundnnd Dover-and Dover 'Cliffs in the *distance ; the ether is a small and exquisitely fin- ! ished group of-Ship's hull and boat, the arawing in ! this latter case being !finished with loving regard and therefore Ainsurpassable. The architectural drawings in colour .(549;562, and 5'681, are all dis- tinguished far their high and detailed !fiiiiSh. They are striking in' this respect, as they are too in the free and certain use of colour. Tire picture numbered riviis apartially finished landseape.which will be of more thannsual interest to those who are , curious to get an insight into some of the processes of a great painter. 'Most of the other' specimens are obviously mere sketches—memoranda of colour for Turner's own use and certainly never intended for exhibition. 'For such a purpose as'they are now on view they are not the less interesting on this account, showing as 'they do how a great artist went about his work in fixing a scene in colours exactly as he saw it. 'Perhaps the most vivid of outline scenes (542) is a foreign one of which En g- lish people can hardly judge. It is a mass of brilliant colour following from the deepest' blue through white, pinks and orange, the whole effect being powerful and suggestive. A river !scene (569) colour Oh blue" shows what can be done with a few touches ot the' brush on a piece 'di' coloured paper. Little as there is of it and on 'it, it is, as it stands—apicture. It may be added that seven pictures 'which are a permanent loan to the Art Gallery have recently been sent tothe National Gallery where they have been thoroughly eles.ned. They have been re- turned, looking all the better for the treatment, and are now again hung on the walls of the Art Gallery. These pictures are :-1. A Farm Yard, by T. C. Cooper, painted in 1834; 2, A. Syrian Maid, contemplating flowers, by 11. W. Pickersgill. R.A. ; '3, Stepping Stones, by' Witherington, R.A.-; 4, Wood Nymph, by T. Phillips, R.A. ; 5, A Dangerous Play- mate, by Etty, R.A: ;' 6, Venice, Sunset (Turner), and 7, a landscape with cattle in water, bythe same (artist.

div.head: SEIOCTING TRAGEDY NEAR RUGBY.
div.p: SEIOCTING TRAGEDY NEAR RUGBY.

On Tuesday night, a shepherd tia.med Dennis, when walking along the canal near Rugby, saw a woman in the tvdter, apparently dead, and two little boys struggling near her. He rescued the bays, who were insensible, but•the woman, on being got out was found to be dead. The'children were restored, and gave the name of their father as Charles Bromwich, Of New Bilt4n, near Rugby. The 'father, on being interviewed, stated :that since his wile was confined, three months ago, she had complained Ipains in the head. Her infant is missing, and is sup- posed to be drowned.

Tt Westbury-on-Severn, on Tuesday, the gmardians -suspended Mrs. Macdonald, schoolmistress at the Wor- khouse, in consequence of serious charges brought against her. It was alleged, among other things, thatshe threw sixteen buckets of water over one girl, and fourteen over another, that she caned boys until their hands tiled, and sometimes beat them when they were naked, that she pushed one boy clown.a flight of fourteen steps, injuring his knee, and that she lashed another's naked body with a bunch of leather laces. div.head: FATHER MAT-HEW CENTENARY.
div.p: THE FATHER MAT-HEW CENTENARY.

A great gathering of members of total abstinence asso- ciations, trade societies, municipal and 'other public bodies took place in Dublin on Monday, to honour the memory of Pather'Mathew, the temperance reformer. A processioa was formed in Stephen's-green„and marched thence to Upper Sackvill-st., where the Laz.d Mayor laid the topmost stone of a pedestal that has been erected midway hltween'the Nelson column and the Rotunda to I receive a statue of Father Mathew. Speeches were then delivered, the speakers including Lord Plunket, the Archbishop of LLblin, the Moderator e the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland, Fathers Nugent and -Keating (representing Cardinal Manning), Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., and Mr. John 'Redmond, M.P. Nearly allthe processionists wore the temperance medal of Father Mathew suspended by a green ribbon.

On tunday=orning the Rev. Dr. Preston, vicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, made the following re- femme to theCiate Mr. li. Timmins, 'whose remains were interred at the Cemetery, on the previous Wednesday. rHe said the town has-lost a most use- ful and ze,aloes townsman, that church and parish a most capable and attached menaLer and philan- thropic parishioner. The late Mr. Ebenezer Tim- mins was a trnze philanthropist. He had a warm heart for the 'distressed, a ready hand to relieve the wanting, a generous disposition, a loving nature, and was-coo to whorl appeal was not naade ,in vain. What Ihe did was not done with affectation, for the sake of , show„-or to will popular applause. He was content to ' do a goad work without proclaiming it,o2 the housetops. He let not his right hand know whathis left hand had performed. He was a man of integrity, of probity, of , unblemished character, and not one could point a finger, and accuse him,of an unworthy act, or of a deed for whichte might Lave blushed. On his character rested no stain. He was wise in counsel, prudent in advice, and for manyryears ha was an official in that church, and was connected with their institutions. His presence at their meetingsthey ever valued. He had a penetra- ting mad, and:grasped the details af amaatter readily, and so was able to give sound advice on the best course to be pursued. As a public man, and a€ a friend, he would be sadly missed, and his place would not be read- ily filled. Ablexenerous, philanthropic, well-disposed men didetot everywhere abound; the worship of self was too common. Would that the liberal.crid generous disposition of their departed friend was more universal, and the Church at large the gainer. He had gone, and they could but say" Thy will be done." It-was pleasing to know blast his kat testimony was" Simply to Thy moss I cling." Over such as thus depart the Holy Spirit had written the epitaph, "Blessed are they that die in the Lord; they lest from their labours, and their works do follow them."

div.head: FUNERAL OF MRS. BOOTH.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MRS. BOOTH.
GREAT GATHERING, AND IMPRESSIVE CEREMONY.

The remains of Mrs. Booth were interred at Abney Park Cemetery, London, on Tuesday afternoon, thedis- play made by the Salvationists being on a most exten- sive scale. The procession was timed to fall in on the Thames Embankment at half-past eleven, but it was a quarter to one before a start was made. There were about 6,000 Salvationists in uniform in the procession, and bands and banners, specially brought for the occa- sion, were numerous. About 30,000 spectators gathered 1 on the Embankment to see the procession start, but al- though the rough element was present, as is always the 1 case with London crowds, the horseplay was far less than usual. At half-past twelve the crowd had become so great that the police stopped all the vehicular traffic. The procession started for Abney Park Cemetery at a quarter to one. It was composed solely of officers of the army, no soldiers or friends being I allowed to join the ranks, but great numbers fol- lowed in its wake. " Commissioner " Carleton was in command of the procession, which was formed in fifteen battalions, each battalion consisting of four com- panies composed as follows :—The male captains march- ing together; the male lieutenants; the female captains, including officers' wives; and the female lieutenants. These came from all parts of the kingdom. There were 4,500 officers belonging to the United Kingdom; and Australia, America, South Africa, France, Belgium, Switzerland, Ceylon, and other countries sent delegates. The procession was led by male cadets, in red jerseys, , carrying the draped colours of a hundred of the chief corps in Great Britain, and foreign representatives carry- ing flags of their countries. Then came the social reform and rescue officers and staff captains. The remains of Mrs. Booth, which had been brought from Olympia., fol- lowed, preceded by the band of the" Household Troops." The coffin was laid on a kind of gun carriage and upon ' its plain oaken lid were placed the bonnet and Bible of Mrs. Booth. All around were gay coloured flags repre- sentative of the countries in which the army carries on its work. Next rode the chief and commandant on horseback, and the carriages of the mourners. " General " Booth was seated in the first carriage, and in the others were "The Marechals," " Field Commis- sioner," Mrs. Booth-Tucker, Miss Lucy Booth, Miss Marie Booth, and other members of the family. Fifty brass bands accompanied the procession, which was remarkable and imposing, and there was an absence of the sombreness attending a funeral cortege. All traffic was suspended as the procession wended its way through the city to Abney Park Cemetery. When both field and staff officers had taken their places, the sounding of the bugle called for attention, and then the coffin was carried to the grave side. After silent prayer, the hymn ." Rock 3f Ages" was sung ; "Major" Musa-Bhai followed with prayer, and then the whole body sang a Salvation Army chorus. Mrs. " Major " Cook having offered prayer, "Staff Captain" Annie Bell sang a solo, "When the roll is called in heaven," while all joined in the stirring chorus. Then the "General" read some passages from Scripture, including many of the verses in the Church of England burial service, and afterwards speeches were made. "Colonel" Dowdle spoke on behalf of the United King- dom, "Colonel" 'Nicol for the United States, " Commissioner " Clibborn for the continent of Europe, and " Commissioner " Tucker on behalf of Asia. "The Marechale " (one of Generalßooth's daugh- ters), Mr. Bramwell 'Booth, Mrs. " Commissioner " Booth-Tucker, and: the " General " also delivered ad- dresses, between each of which a chorus was sung. The coffin was then lowered into the grave by six officers , next in rank to the "General" during the singing of onel of the Army songs. ' Commissioner" Railton read a form of service beginning—" Is it has pleased Almighty God to promote our dear mother from her place in the Salvation Army to the mansion prepared for her above, we now commit her body to the grave," and ending with a petition for blessing otrthe Army, which was answered by aloud and prolonged "Amen." Then, while still standing at the graveside, " Colonel " 'Lawley recited a stirring pledge of allegiance to the Army, which was re- peated by allthe officers. After another song, com- mencing " Tothe front, the cry is ringing," the "Gene- ral" pronounced the Benediction, and thus terminated a remarkable scene, both in-respect of the funeral pageant and the singular ceremony substituted for the ordinary service at the graveside.
