div.head: EXECUTION OF 11 PIRATES.
div.p: EXECUTION OF 11 PIRATES.

An Amoy paper reports the execution of eleven Chinese pirates, whose junk was captured by a gunboat. The same journal chronicles the seizure of a trading junk by another pirate craft, and the massacre of her crew of 39 hands.

div.head: KILLED BY A RAM.
div.p: KILLED BY A RAM.

An elderly woman named Ecob, living near Notting- ham, left home on Saturd-ty afternoon to gather sticks. On Sunday her body was found in a neighbouring field, life being extinct. A ram was engaged in butting at the lifeless form, having inflicted fearful injuries. The animal afterwards attacked a policeman, and knocked him down.

div.head: TIPPERARY TRIALS.
div.p: THE TIPPERARY TRIALS.

The Court sat again at Tipperary on Saturday, but no progress was made with the examination of witnesses. One or two matters of interest were, however, decided. Mr. Ronan, on behalf of the Crown, proposed to go on with the case' notwithstanding the absence of Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien. He argued that, the absence of these gentlemen being through their own fault, the method suggested would be perfectly regular. Mr. Healy , protested against the course, but the Bench ruled in , favour of the Crown. A doctor having deposed that Mr. O'Mahony was again too ill to attend, Mr. Ronan asked the Court to proceed with the case in his absence, the Crown undertaking to give no evidence against him while he was away. Strong opposition to this course was offered, and the Bench decided against the Crown, their view being that the case of Mr. O'Mahony was different from that of the two defendants who had deliberately absented themselves. The charge being one of conspir- acy, in which the evidence affected all the defendants, and Mr. O'Mahony being away from the court through no fault of his own, an adjournment became necessary. The Court was then adjourned. The special correspondent of the Press Association wired on Monday that the deadlock in the Tipperary trials still continued. At the sitting of the Court medi- cal evidence was given to show that the defendant 011ahony cculd not possibly attend for some days. Mr. Ronan, on behalf of the Crown, asked for an adjourn- ment until Tuesday, when he undertook to suggest a course which would enable the case to bc proceeded with despite the absence of the invalid. Mr. Redmond ob- jected to such a short adjournnent, but the Bench granted the application. On Tuesday the magistrates sailed into calm water, at least for the present, and, after a delay of eleven days, the examination of Constable Lenane, who was giving evidence when scene occurred which led to Mr. Harrington's retirement from the ease, was resumed and concluded. Previous to this, Mr. Ronan applied that Mr. O'Mahony should be dismissed from the case without prejudice,which was done. Then Mr. Healy argued that, as the case was one of conspiracy, the whole of the defendants should now be discharged. The bench, how- ever, saw no reason why the proceedings should be further interrupted, and a quantity of police evidence was heard during the day. On Wednesday several witnesses for the Crown gave evidence. Mr. Healy objected to the effort being made to connect Mr. John Dillon and Mr. W. O'Brien with the alleged conspiracy for which John Kelly and Malachi O'Dwyer were in prison, and, apart from the question of the legality of the course the Crown was pursuing, he urged that the bulk of the evidence should be freduced, saying they were prepared to take their sentences on muchness evidence. Mr. Ronan, at a later stage, pro- tested against Mr. Healy's interruptions, and said they would not induce him to omit a line of testimony.

div.head: ARRIVAL OF MR. DILLON AND MR. O'BRIEN IN FRANCE.
div.p: ARRIVAL OF MR. DILLON AND MR. O'BRIEN IN FRANCE.

SIX DAYS AT SEA. A telegram received at Dublin, at one o'clock on Wed- nesday afternoon announced the safe arrival of Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., and Mr. John Dillon, M.P., at Cherbourg, on the French coast. Their journey has occnpied longer than was expected. They were over six days at sea, while the journey under favourable circum- stances should only have occupied half that time. It was with feelings of great relief that the news of their safe arrival was received in Ireland. How did they get away? That is the question everyone is asking. Curio- sity cannot be gratified at present, for the Government intend, it is said, to pounce upon all who aided and abetted in their escape. Suffice it to say that shortly after midnight on Wednesday last Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Dillon drove down in a closed car- riage to the river side. A boat awaited them, and they were conveyed across the Liffey to a craft rid- ing at her moorings. A few friends assembled, on the beach to witness their departure, and anxiously they waited until the yacht moved past the coastguard station and safely out into the Irish Sea. The wind was westerly, and seemed favourable; but in reality it was almost dead against the craft which was making down channel. The prolonged journey is thus accounted for, taken together with the fact that the wind during the past week has at no period been strong. They struck the nearest port which the French coast' presented to them. Running free they made a good passage until Guernsey was reached, and then passing in through the Channel group, they reached Cherbourg, where they dis- embarked early on Wednesday, and communicated their safe arrival to Dublin. Their point of landing leaves them only a short railway journey to Havre, whence they propose to start for America within the next few days. Another telegram from Dublin states that Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien arrived in France. On Wednesday morning the yacht in which they left Ireland sailed into Cherbourg harbour. The hon. gentlemen landed at the quay, and proceeded to one of the hotels in the town. Cherbourg is within easy distance of the 'port of flavra, from which American steamers start. Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien will remain at Cherbourg for a day or two. Mrs. O'Brien who awaited in Dublin the news of her hus- band's safe arrival, was much delighted at the receipt Of a telegram from him on Wednesday afternoon, and left i Dublin on Wednesday night to join her husband. It is proposed to give the fugitives a great welcome in America, and a meeting of all the Irish societies is being held to arrange the details of their reception, which will include the despatch of a special tug down the harbour to meet the steamer, and a meeting in some hall in New York, at which a series of speeches will be delivered. In the opinion of the Irish in New York, Mr. Dillon 1 and Mr. O'Brien may expect to raise 250,000 dollars in this country. The friends of the Irish movement are try- ing to arrange for the 69th Regiment, which is com- manded by Colonel Cavanagh, who is an Irishman, to meet the refugees at theißattery,and escort them to their , hotel. IN PARIS.

Messrs. Dillon and O'Briem arrived in Paris on Thurs- day morning, and the latter, in the course of an inter- view with a Press representative, mentioned that Mr. Dillon and he left the mouth of the Liffey on the evening of the Bth inst., in a small yacht owned by Mr. John Clancy. Mr. O'Brien described the incidents of the voyage, which were somewhat exciting, and added that in leaving Ireland as they did they had no other end in view than to keep their engagements in the United States. They proposed to remain eight days in Paris, and then sail from Havre to New York.

During Wednesday night the wind from the northwest increased in strength, and was accompanied by heavy showers of rain and sleet and hail. Off Liverpool the fury of the gale was felt by the steamers from Dublin and Belfast.— The timber-laden ship W. H. Corsar, from St. John' N. 8., and belonging to Messrs.W.H. Dickson and C0.,0f Liver- pool, anchored in the river on Wednesday night off New Brighton, but early next morning broke away from her. ; moorings, losing her anchors, and t9;;;x thO 001:111d or the Magazines bank. Tfl6lo relbained until the tugs Universe and Ethea,i'd Finch towed her off. While she was in the lVr her foretopsail was blown to ribbons. seme storm visited the Peak district of Derbyshire on Wednesday night, with much lightning. A SCHOONER IN DANGER. The schooner Richard, of Runcorn, laden with coal, from Whitehaven to Killough, encountered a fearful gale on Wednesday night. She was driven towards the west coast of the Isle of Man, and was sighted off Peel, her sails blown to shreds, and drifting towards Peel Castle rocks. A lifeboat was quickly manned and put out. The crew were put on board, ropes were made fast, and eventually she was hauled into the harbour. She was half full of water. Great excitement prevailed. WRECK OF A NAVAL STEAM LAUNCH. EXCITING SCENE. A terrific gale raged off Holyhead. The steam launch from H.M.S. Neptune, guardship at Holyhead, was bring- ing ashore leave men, and when attempting to land at the slip she was staved in, and began to settle down. A scene of great excitement occurred, bluejackets and marines being precipitated into the water, which was very turbulent, but eventually they were all got ashore.

A " TIFF " AT THE COUNTY POLICE

COURT. It is a very unusual proceeding for a member of the bar to wax ire in open Court at the sitting magistrates. The occurrence, however, happened during the progress of the County Police Court on Wednesday. The magistrates, Messrs. W. H. Bleck- ly (presiding), and Z. Armitage, had disposed of several cases as they appeared on the charge sheet —that is in rotation—but when they came to an assault case in which Mr. Wilson, solicitor, repre- sented the defendant, they ignored the rule, and called forth another case which necessitated two magistrates to try it, in order that one—Mr. Armit- age—who evidently was heavily pressed with busi- ness affairs, might leave the court at a certain time. It was this deviation which Mr. Wilson emphatically objected to. He was getting eloquent in his oratory, which throughout contained animadversion ; when the chairman asked him to allow the hearing of one more case before his. The Clerk next interposed and said he could get on much quicker if Mr. Wil- son would not be so locquacious; but the gentleman smartly retaliated by retorting that he could do absolutely nothing, except waste his time which was, he averred, as important as that of the gentle- men who were responsible for law and order. Mr. Wilson again strongly protested to the magisterial "shelving," and he particularly laid stress on the fact that he was asking no favour. The magistrates, however, were immovable, and peremptorily decided to go on with the next case. This only caused Mr. Wilson's fire of chagrin to burn more , furiously; and, at last, after resorting to all fair and ' lawful means to persuade the magistrates that his claim was justifiable, but without effect, he sat down to await his turn ; but not before designating the decision of the Bench improper and unfair.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. OCTOBER 18, 1890.
Balfouz Baffled.
THE IRISH SECRETARY will be able to add an interesting chap-

ter to his work on "Philosophic Doubt; for if he is anything of a philosopher he will certainly be something of a doubter when he reflects, on the mess that he has made of it by his latest, futile attempt to crush the leaders of the Home-Itule party in Ireland. It was very pleasant for him, to, be sure, to listen to the rumours about the dissensions of the Nationalists, and the oppor- tunity which was thus given him of overpowering the National League. He has tried again, and he hasagain failed. Men who play golf in Scotland, and get their information second-hand, are sure to blunder about Ireland. So far is MR. BALFoun from overpowering the League that it looks as if the League would be likely to overpower him. The Tipperary prosecutions began tragically enough; but the Irish, who can laugh as well as cry, have converted them into a farce. It was very pretty in theory to prevent MR. JOHN DILLoN and Mn. WILLIAM O'BRIEN from keeping their engage- ments in America by putting them in gaol in Ireland; but, pretty as the theory was, it has not proved practicable. The birds are not to be caged this time; they have flown. The Lisa SECRETARY ought to have known that Mr. O'BRIEN has a way of keeping his engagements, notwith- standing all the efforts to prevent him of all the Irish constabulary; he should have remembered Manchester. Messrs. DILLON and O'BRIEN have had enough of the mockery of justice which is offered at Tipperary; they prefer to lay their case before the free citizens of the United States; and there is every reason to believe that, embarking from France, they will soon be on their way thither. Mr. BALFOUR like another Glendower, may seek to call their spirits from the vasty deep; but the question is--Will they come when he doth call on them?

Disappointed and discomfited, the Coercionista would turn moralists and preach against the sin committed by Messrs. DitLoN and O'BetEN US leaving the country when they are "out on bail." But that is a matter between theta and the persons who have become bail for them, and we do not anticipate that thell will cry shame on the Irish leaders for proceeding to America to advocate the Irish cause. It is open of course for easy-chair politicans to say that Messrs. Dllakisz and O'BRIEN have run away because they were afraid of prison punishment ; and it is equally open for men of common-sense to decide whether they believe this is their motive, seeing that both men have in the past again and again gone to prison rather than move one hair's breadth from the line they have adopted. It is surely a simple explanation to say that both gentle- men were under engagement to address meetings in America in aid of famine-stricken peasants, ag well as on behalf of the National League, and that they prefer to keep those engagements rather than walk into the pit which Mr. BALFOUR 110 ilug for them. Granted that they will have to come back, that the end is not yet, that there is the question to be faced of paying the L 2,000 bail which may be forfeited. and With regard to the cash, there will be no difficulty under the circumstances of raising the amount in America—if need be many times over. But it is by no means certain as yet that the sureties are under obligation to meet the cal' upon them for £2,000. Their bond was to pro- duce Messrs. Dim..ex and O'BRIEN on a sPeeifie, date to answer a specific charge. They dischargee their responsibility by producing both these gentlemen on the day named ; and the Court then proceeded to repair its blunders by altering tha charge against the prisoners. An altered charge is a new accusation,and the question arises whether, under the altered circumstances, it was not neeea- sary to enter into fresh bail on the adjourn" ment of the court. Mr. HEALY contends that it was, and Mr. HEALY has very often proved to be right. If Smith becomes suretY for, Jones who is charged with murder, is he still Winn if the charge be altered to one of burglarY ? It does not seem unreasonable to suPl)°,,..ag that his responsibility ceases when the charge Is altered. But it is contended on behalf of the Crown that the change in the case in question was so small that it does not affect the bail. That, I however, is a point of law which will have to be i argued before a court higher in standing than that presided MI Ity thq Rumovables. Metaliirna Messrs. DutoN and O'Bratx are bent on their errand of mercy, well pleased that they "lava been able once more to baffle Mr. BALFOUR.

AN. American poet has told us Mayors' "HANS BRIETMANN gave a Parth, Dinners, and how the moral of the whow trouble and cost was summed up in the question "Where is that party now ?" There is a Hans hl every borough who, as Mayor for the time being/ feels constrained to give a party to fellow-members of the Corporation, and who doubtless puts tho question to himself, as he thinks of the bill and head in the morning—" Where is that party now The custom is one which would be more honoureu by the breach than by the observance; and we are looking forward to a Chief Magistrate who will he wise enough and strong enough to disregard cur tom in the matter, and have the courage to spend such money as he is willing to part with, in a WO which will be permanently beneficial to the inhabit" ants at large. The expense of dinner-giving certainly a small matter to the magnates who ale usually called upon to direct the corporate affair° of our large towns and cities, and it is due t° such men to say that as a rule it forms but a minor part of their bounties. But in smaller places, line Warrington* the Mayor's Dinner often looms so large in the Mayoral expenditure as to be the means of shutting oft many a fi/s pound note which would otherwise probably go t° some deserving object. The MAYOR of Warring' ton (Alderman FRANCOIIB) has given a dinner this week which will cost him a good share of a hundred peunds, notwithstanding the limited provision consequent on the large number who were unable to, accept the invitation. As he has not dis" tinguished himself during his year of office either by gifts or in any other way, we cannot but thin)r he would have done better if he had devoted eke money to the Infirmary Extension, the Grins' sium Fund, or even by adding a picture to the Art Gallery; for alas, now that the "feed and the fuddle" are over, the question will arise—"Whe,,r° is that party now ?" And they do eat, and drill'? and, smoke at Mayors' dinners; for there are Pee- ple, even amongst those have attained to the exalted rank of Town Councillor, who have et weakness for overloading the ship to the I)(Thu of disaster when there is no charge for the carg?' The present writer has attended one Malres„: dinner only at Warrington; it was some ago, and it was enough. One Alderman filled hint' self so full that before he left the table his a°9- tomy revolted. The stomach was wiser than the man. Whether the performance was repeated ertt Thursday we are unable to say; for the presen MAYOR has introduced a custom of his own bi limiting the favour of his invitations—if favour can be called—to one local paper. His WershiPt styles himself a Conservative and a Churchman, bud he has overlooked even the organ of his church an his party. Perhaps he intends it to be understood, now that he has made full use of the party ladtir that for tho future he must be regarded as "nent'i in all matters political and. religious." It cariu°* be that he has confined himself to one PoPs" because of any doubt as to room for the represent*. tives of the two other papers, seeing,. as alreaci/ suggested, not a few who were invited wrote to so); they could not be present. And it is n° to be supposed that Alderman FueNcOtert thinks for a moment of getting a reP° "on the cheap," for is it not notorious that he has been wonderfully successful this year in 111° " financial operations ? It simply comes to this, w suppose, that it is his way of doing things; but .t is a way, as he may yet learn, which is neither courteous nor dignified, but calculated rather to bring discredit upon himself and upon the offic° which he holds. But having reached this pitch, it will perhaps give the quietus to that post-prandial self-glorification which inevitably ends in sinok,e• If that should be the case—if the latest IVIaPr s Dinner should prove to be the last, Aldernlani FRANCOMB, will, by accident, have distinguisheu himself, and rendered a service to Warrington.

Young colliers are now-a-days being afforded opportunities which their fathers never dreamed of. At Haydock there is a Mining School, and on zSaturday evening there was a prize distribution to a creditable number of successful students. "More light" amongst miners means in the end more money and less .loss of life.

Here ie a tragedy in brief which may yet form the basis of a three-volume novel:—" ANew York correspondent writes :—Advices from England say that the aunt of Robert Cole, in Southampton, has left him a large fortune. The good news came too late, as Cole cut his throat on Monday in Louisville, Kentucky, in a fit of despondency over poverty."

There can be no doubt as to the approaching famine in the West of Ireland through the failure of the potato crop; but the " Times " for party purposes is doing all it can to minimise it. It is feared that if the people of this. country turn their attention, as they ought, to the distress in the sister isle, they will not listen at the same time to proposals for buying out Irish landlords. Nor should they.

The Chief-Constable considerately explained to the Warrington Magistrates, on Monday, how it became necessary in one case for a policeman to use his staff. He had been hardly used, and drew it and used it in self-defence. This is as it should be ; but how different from the way they have in Ireland! The Irish constabulary don't wait until they are beset; at a hint from a Removable they "go for" harmless people, and risk breaking their truncheons in breaking heads. But their days as bludgeon-men are numbered.

An inquest was held in London, on Tuesday, on the body of a suicide named Sydney Clay. He was a man of 36 years of age, who had had a sun- stroke in India; but the immediate cause of the depression which led him to take his life was the loss, in the streets, of a pet dog. He loved his toy terrier, and, looking to the future,thought perhaps with the "untutored Indian" that- -admitted to that equal sky His favourite dog might bear him company.

Mrs. Hannah Newbrook, widow of the late' "Sammy Buttercup" has again married, or, as " Sammy " would have said," hoo's clogged ageon.' This Lancashire metaphor is understood to have reference to a pair of clogs being soled for the second time ; but there is a word-hunter of our ac- quaintance who will have it that what is meant is that a wife is a clog, and that, on marrying a second time, she " clogs again." It is needless to say that the philologlist in question is "a crusty old bachelor."

The shorthand class in connection with the Warrington Recreative Evening Schools Associa- tion has made a good start; and it is to be hoped the pupils will stick to it. In the days that are coming, the clerk who cannot write shorthand will have to take a seat very much at the back. Shorthand is more generally useful than French or German; but, acquired along with one or the other of these languages, it is an immense advantage to -the young men who would rise in the world "from their dead selves to higher things."

Mr. John Crosfield has ceased to be an alderman of the Borough of Warrinf.T.,t?n.. He has sent in his resignation along with a shilling to cover the re- quisite fine; and there is reason to fear that several other of the older Aldermen will follow suit. The Council can ill afford to lose such men as Mr. Cros- field ; for he has had large experience, and is as far removed from petty tricks and self-seeking as light is from darkness. He spoke last year of resigning ; but was induced to defer his decision on the matter. Who will the Tory majority elect to . fill his seat F Can they rise above party and select the best man P•

The Emperor William means business as a Socialist. He is about to erect 4000 working-men's houses built in a suburb of Berlin, with the object of their becoming the r roperty of the occupants. The rent will not be large, but it will provide for a redemption of the capital. Further, at his sugges- tion, special workmen's trams are about to be run, at low fares, between the city and the outskirts 'Where the workmen reside. The Emperor evi- dently believes with Lord Rosebury that "the politics of the present and the future are the Politics of the poor."
Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien are to sail from France for America oti Saturday next. Meantime they are enjoying themselves in Paris, where

shadows" cease from troubling and constabulary are at rest. Q uestioned fry a correspondent as to the Government asking for their tradition, Mr. Dillon said :—" That would be a stop which would not have the remotest chance of success. I should hope they would be ashamed of such a thing.. England, for so long the champion a liberty, asking France to give up two British members of Parliament I believe we are the only instance of members of the English Parliament being political refugees in a foreign country."

There is no room to question the sincerity of the Salvationists in their mourning for the loss-of Mrs. Booth, whose unique personality, splendid preach- ing power, and womanly tenderness drew them towards her as the Mother of the Army. Good sense was shown in robbing death of some of its terrors by making the funeral comparatively-cheer- ful, The Salvationists could say with Gerald Massey:—
Strange glory streams through Mee wild rents, And, through the open door of death We see the heaven that beckoneth

growing rapidly, for it is estimated that it will be found to touch 35,000 when the census is taken next year. The rateable value has increased in a like proportion. In 1881, it was £102,000 ; to-day it is £138,000. There are few towns of such a size and importance that have not become Municipal boroughs; and it is fitting, therefore, that the inhabitants of Widnes hould again consider Whether the time has not arrived when they should make another step in advance. The question was under consideration at a meeting of the Local Board, on Tuesday, and it was unanimously resolved that the opinion of the ratepayers be ' ascertained by a house to house canvass. This is:a course which is strongly to be commended, for the issue is too important to be left to the decision of a meeting which might be indifferently attended, as others have been, and thus prove no safe guide as to the opinion of the town as a whole. It is satis- factory to observe that the information which has been obtained as to the rating side of the question does not by any means load to the conclusion that government by a Corporation will necessarily be more costly than government by a Local Board. It depends less upon the mode of government than upon the men governing. It is true that rates have increased in the majority of the towns that have been incorporated; but it is not unlikely that they would have increased if the same places had remained under the authority of Local Boards, and carried out similar improve- ments. The Clerk to the Widnes Local Board pointea out, on Tuesday, that in one respect the town would gain by the change. At present, land and railways are entitled to a large deduction from the District Rate; but there would be no discount from the rate levied by a borough. This may be thought to be hard on landowners and railway .companies ; but as these powerful bodies get the Pull in so many other ways it is not a matter about -which the ratepayers at anyrate need break their hearts. There can be no question as to this—that a municipality will be in position to act with more :freedom and more power. They will have their own affairs more completely in their own hands; ,and it will depend upon themselves whether they 'do well or ill. Widnes is a chemical centre, and, 4uffering as it does from noxious fumes, it requires ‘to be watched and protected from a health point Taf wiew in every possible way. A Town Council can do more to minimise the evil than a Local Board, especially if is backed by strong expressions 'of opinion on the part of the inhabitants. O'KEEFEE would probably find, too, that there Would be less reason to complain, as he has had occasion to do, of the abomination of stinking garbage of all kinds being thrown on the roads, for, if Mr. BROWN could "not smell anything" 'there might be others on the Sanitary Committee 'with noses equal to the occasion. It is a strong thing for Dr. O'KEEFFE to say that the Board is not doing its duty in regard to public health ; and, if it be so, the sooner there is a Corporation the better it will be for the town.

If one policeman can prove that alabourer is , drunk, how many police officers are required to prove that a veterinary surgeon is intoxicated ? The answer is, that nobody can tell, after-the bear- ing of a case bearing on the point at St. Helens, on Monday. P.C. Turton swore that he saw Mr. Menzies, veterinary surgeon, drunk witilst in charge of a horse and carriage, and P.S: Charlton and P.S. Hudson corroborated; but, as sundry witnesses who were called, expressed another opi- nion, the case was dismissed. Wonder if Mr. Menzies, if lie had been a carter, would have' got the benefit of the doubt?

The Scottish Home Rule Association are press- ing Mr. Gladstone hard for an expression of opinion during his forthcoming campaign; but it showld be remembered that Mr. Gladstone's rule as a statesman is "one thing at a time." He is pledged to Home Rule for Ireland as the first plank in the Liberal platform, and cannot be expected- to burden himself with a new agitation. Let Scotch- men, by all means, keep pegging away with the advocacy of their scheme. If they are as shrewd as they used to be, they must know that granting Home Rule for Ireland is the speediest way of ob- taining it for Scotland—and for Wales and Eng- land.

Sir William Houldsworth is amongst the Con- servatives who are looking ahead on the licensing question. Speaking at Preston, on Monday, ho said :—" The licensing laws were completely anti ,- gusted, and not suited to the requirements of the day. What we required were licensing boards; elected so as to represent the feelings of the people, and to place in their hands the whole of the licen- sing question and the regulation of the public- houses. These boards must take care that licenses were the exception, and not the rule, and we must diminish very greatly the licenses at presentin existence." Diminish very greatly "—that is a phrase which licensing magistrates, who desire to do their duty, should ever have in mind.

It has come out as one result of the Tipperary proceedings that even Mr. John Morley was. "noted" as suspect by one constable. Then as to "shadowing," this is tho confession of a constable on Tuesday :—" He followed them everywhere, he'l could, and took a note of any conversation he could hear. He stopped as near to those he was follow- ing as circumstances would permit. It was part of his duty to look into the windows of private houses and shops to see what people wore doing. Hie I went into Mr. Carew's public-house in Tipperary, and upstairs to a private room." A nice way truly of maintaining law and order! If the people of Ireland were strong enough, they would' be justified in rising in revolt against such tyranny:.

A HARMONIC SOCIETY FOR WIDNES. A meeting, with the object of organising a harmonic Society for Widnes, was held at the Grosvenor Hotel on Wednesday. Mr. S. SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY AT WIDNES. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, yesterday, held an inquest at Widnes Police Station, on the body of Elizabeth Dean, aged eight months, daughter of William Dean, of Birchfield Cottages. On Wednesday the mother left the infant in the cradle, and when she returned, she found a piece of burning paper on its forehead. Her son, aged one year and eight months was in the room, and it is supposed had been playing with the burning paper. The infant was placed under the care of Dr. Hutchinson, but died on Thursday. A verdict of "Acci- dental death" was returned. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.--. 7. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adrt.

ROBBERY OF JAM AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, James Hard- man, Lugsdale-road, and Thomas Brett, Midwood-st., young men, were charged on remand with having last Monday stolen six pots of jam from a lurry belonging to John William Woods. It was alleged that they com- mitted the offence when the lurry was at Ditton, the 3fiVer having given them a "lift." When apprehended Hardman said that he had found three pots of jam in the road.—Mr. W. Knowles, for the defence, urged that a prima fecie case had not been made out, though he ad- mitted that there were suspicious circumstances in regard to the conduct of Hardman.—Both were in drink at the time.—The bench said that they considered the case proved against Hardman, but as he had previously borne a good character, they would only impose a fine of 205., including costs. They also thought that Brett must have had a guilty knowledge, and should fine him 10s., including costs. LAMPS, choice designs.—Garland's Lamp Shops. Barlestown cud Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: ASSAULT ON A GAMES:LEPER AT CNONTON.
div.p: ASSAULT ON A GAMES:LEPER AT CNONTON.

John Wright, Chapel-lane, and Francis Edward were each summoned for assaulting Henry Andrews, at Crou- ton, on the sth inst. Mr. Knowles prosecuted, and stated that on the day in question the two defendants with two other men, were going along Tarbock-road, Cronton,with a rabbit deg. A little boy seeing the dog trespassing near a fence, threw a stone at it. Edwards then got hr.lel of the boy and shook him, and the boy's mother (Mrs. Andrews) seeing the act, interferred. The prosecutor, who was in the woods close by, heard the noise, and came up and spoke to the defendants. Edwards, after saying what he could do, struck at An- drews, andseized him by his beard. In the struggle which followed, Edwards bit Andrews' thumb, which had since been dressed by a doctor, and whilst on the ground. Wright interferred and struck the prosecutor on the left side of the face. Mrs. Andrews, in attempting to release her husband, was also struck by the defend- ants. Evidence was given in support of this statement. and Edwards was fined 40s. and costs. Wright was ordered to pay 20s. and costs.

Thomas Scott, a labourer was summoned for assault- ing John Sweeney, on Wednesday, the Ist October. The comp4ainant said he lodged at Scott's. On the night in question. Scott and his wife had been drinking at the Barley Mow, and he was running her round the house in order to get some money from her, when he came across witness, whom he struck on the head with a stick, and also blacked his eyes. In answer to Mr. Burton, who defended, complainant said on the Tuesday, Lincoln Jack's wife struck him on the head with a fender, but she did not black his eyes. On the Wedndsday there was a.row, and he "struck to make peace"; hut had not a fight with Lincoln Jack. Mr. Burton pointed out that the defendant had met with an accident on the Ship Canal, and his spinal cord was injured, and the pelvis bone broken, and he could not stand or walk without two sticks. A child could knock him down. Witnesses were called to prove that Sweeney's face was scratched, and both his eyes blacked by Lincoln Jack, and that Sweeney was drunk at the time. The summons was dismissed. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-it.. Warrington.—Advt. BRAVERY REWARDED AT WIDNES.

An interesting ceremony -tOoTi place at the Baths Assembly Booms, Widnes, on Tuesday evening, when Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, J.P., presented the Royal Humane Society's bronze medal and certificate to Joseph Owen, a. youth, 15 years of age, for saving the life of a boy named John Foster, 11 years of age. On the evening of the 28th July, Foster fell into the river at the promenade, and he was rapidly carried away by the strong flowing tide. A boy named Worthington jumped into the water but found he could not swim with his clothes on, and all hopes of saving the life of the drowning boy were given up, when Owen dived into the river, and, after a tremen- dous struggle, brought the boy safely to the shore. Speeches were made by Mr. James Morrison and Mr. E. Carey, the latter gentleman remarking that the Local Board were doing all they could to have the dangerous state of the river side remedied.—Mr. Deacon in making the presentation, eulogised Owen's courage and skill as a swimmer, and said he had done his duty bravely and suc- cessfully.—Owen briefly returned thanks and Mr. J. Hartland spoke on behalf of the father of the rescued boy. It was stated that the matter was brought under the notice of the Royal Humane Society by Mir. T. Atherton, junr. MARRIAGE OF MR. J. div.p: If VIOLENT, MAN AT WIDNES..

At Widnes Police Court. en Tuesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington, P. McCabe, 78 Orford-st., was charged with doing wilful damage to the extent of £B, to the property of Joseph Rickey, labourer. In July last the prisoner married Hickey's daughter and had since lived with his father-in-taw. The houso was furnished on the hire: system with the exception of one bed which belonged ta the prisoner. Cn returning, home on Monday morning, after being at work alt night, Hickey found nearly the whole of the furniture smashed and a portion of it burned. It transpired that on Sunday night the prisoner was in the street in search of his wife and he threat- ened that if he did nob find her, he would set the house on fcre and he appeared to have attempted to carry out histhreat. When apprehended by P.C. 225 he admitted' that he had smashed the furniture, but alleged that it I was his own, having been given to him by Hickey. Witnesses proved the furniture belonged to the latter, and the prisoner was committed for trial at Liverpool Quarter Sessions. On Wednesday McCabe was.brought before Mr. Deacon charged with having unlawfully wounded a labourer named Hickey. The prosecutor said that shortly before eleven o'clock on Monday morn- ing he was watching some boys playing at football near Oxford-st.. when the prisoner came up and4said " Are you the liting man ? " Witness replieth that ha did not want anything to do with him an the prisoner struck him on the face with his fist and then knocked him down with another blow. On getting up, witness said he would fight the prisoner fah:up ".but he did not get a chance as the prisoner got hint on the 'Poor, and kickel him on the hips, back and right hand several times. The prisoner was wearing dogs with pointed toes. In answer to prisoner, witness, said he had no Quarrel with him and had not offeped to fight him any- where. Dr. O'Keefe deposed that the prosecutor was severely bruised. The prisoner was committed for trial. - COLLIERY Fikle,rxrg. - - -

Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an in- quest at the Wagon and Horses Hotel, Haydock, on ' Monday afternoon, on the body of W. Boden, a col- lier, of 139, Earle-st., Earlestown. The deceased was employed in the Queen Pit, of Messrs. Evans and Co., Haydock. and OA Tuesday, the 7th inst., he was jammed between a runaway wagon and others which were standing the pit. He was taken to the Cottage Ilospitat, but he was so terribly in- jured that his life was despaired of, and he died in that institution on Sunday morning. A verdict of "Accidental (loth" was retuned,

Putp.wonits ix A HATDOCR COAL. Prr. A case that illustrates from what slight causes disasters may arise came before the magistrates of the Newton-he-Willows Potty Sessional sitting at thaNewton Tovrn.llall, on Saturday. A younglad named Ralph Shenton, 15 years a age, whose thoughts would naturally run in the direction of pleasure rather than of work, was charged with having, on the 25th or September, contravened the regulatiOns in regard to coal mines, by taking with him into the Boston Pit, Haydock, a number of ex- plbsiYis substances, to wit, fireworks. It would appear fromthe circitmstartces of the case that the lad, taking time hy the forelock, was laying in a :stook of fireworks in retviiness for Guy Fawkes' day' Being apprehensive, however, that some of his com- panions might try to obtain surreptitious possession of them, he determined to keep them closely under his own. control, and when he went to work in the pit he took the fireworks with him. The prosecu- tionovhich was not taken vindictively, was con- ducted by Mr Stuart, solicitor, who explained that the colliery proprietors, Messrs. Evans and Co., simply wished it to be made known that such dangerous proceedings could not be allowed. He remarked that on the day named in the charge, Thomas Marsh, a fireman in the employ of the Com- pany. found that the defendant had a quantity of ttrevrorks Chinese crackers in his possession. Shenton told him he was afraid some one might take them, and that was the reason he had brought them down the pit. Mr. Stuart added that he was instructed not to press for an exemplary penalty, as the authorities thought the lad had acted thought- lessly. Regulations were made with the special object of protecting the lives of workers in mines. and it was very often found that the workers them- selves were the last persons to assist the managers of collieries in protecting their own lives. The set- ting off of one cf these fireworks might have en- dangered the lives of a great many people. The masters were not vindictive in these prosecutions, but it was absolutely necessary that they should be taken for the safety of life. He would only ask for the costs. The Chairman of the magistrates ',Mr. T. J. Gillespie) characterised the action of the defen- dant as very stupid, and said that they could not impose a less fine than one of 10s. and costs.

FINANCE. The Finance Committee recommended the payment of lbccounts amounting to t 3,449 I. Passed. THE. PROPOSED INCORPORATION. The General Purposes Committee recommended that the oplrdon of the ratepayers be ascertained by a house to house canvass, and if found favourable that applica- tion be made for a charter.—The Clerk read a long com- munication, signed by Mr. Bowfin, from the Widnes Branch of the Irish National League strongly advocat- ing incorporation.—Mr. Delaney who had made inquiries on the subject forwarded the replies of the Mayor of St. Helens, the Mayor of Warrington, and the Mayor of Bootle.—Mr. Bishop declined to state whether a town was better governed by a Corporation or a Local Board., He believed the ratepayers were the best judges.—Mr_ , Francomb said a Corporation would have very much more power, and the town would be very much better, governed.—Mr. King was strongly in favour of incorpcgt ation.—The Clerk said he had been instructed to mckis inquiries into the subject and he had visited Nelson and Eccles. From information supplied at the latter place, he found that out of 18 boroughs, the rates in 15 bad been increased, and in three they had been decressed, but none would say that the increase or decrease had been caused through incorporation; the said it had arisen through carrying out works which-would have been carried out by a Local Board. There would also be an improvement in the book-keePing for the township. As to whether the rotes. of Widnes would be increased, he had made an estimate based on last year's expenses, of what would have been the borough rate. They now had a general district rate Of 2.5. ed., and he estimated that the borough mite would have been 2s. s}d. on the expenses for the year eading. March, 1891. From this it appeared the town would: benefit from incorporation. That arose in th.:/...way. The borough rate would be charged upon land and railways,. just the same as the poor rate, while on the general dia. trict rate they had to allow a discount a three-f °laths to land, railways, and canals, which simply. paid oa one. quarter of the rateable value.—Mr. Carey,,ip moving the adoption of the minute. said the Committee had come to the conclusion that there was no proof that incorporation would increase the rates ; and that being so, the strong. eat objection of several members waa removed and the Committee came to the conclusicn to ascertain, the opinion of the ratepayers.—Dr. onleeffe seconded, the motion; and said lie had been hammering for thissfor seven years.—The motion was cazded unanitnously.,--It was also resolved that the followittg officials of the Board should conduct the canvass, according to a scheme ar- ranged by the Clerk :—Messrs. The second of the-course of lectures on. " pre- blems of wealth and industry," was delivered in. Bethesda Lecture Halli.on Thursday evening, by Mr..- Hubert Llewellyn Smith, B.A.A, Sc. The weather was very wet and stormy, and adversely affected the audienceawhich Was-not so hirge as usual. The subject for the evening weir "'The problem of production —Land labour, and capital:" The Lecturer saiciaand, labour,and capitaLliad been the watchword of bitte:a con- troversies whiah. were new raging, but they should endeavour to keep outside those controversies, • and rEgard land labour and capital co-operat, log together to make wealttn.rather than as competing together for a share of wealthwhen it is made. Wealth was the product of Man's labourovorWng upon the raw materials of nature.-land—andthey would have to ask: about the law of productive power of land, and the law of tbe productive ?ewer. of labour. But if they looked: at the industrial work of a vast civilized com- munity such as ours, they- did not find things so . simple—they did net find people simply working up raw material into • wealtb. They were constantly working not upon raw material:but upon the results of past labour. In the- mill, in tke- workshop, in the field, men were constantly,- labouring' upon results of other - people labour—the eored upe energy of past labour was called in to prodboe productive power of labour to- day. So important oms this • use of the accumulated results of the past labour that it was usual to give its definite name and it was often spoken-of ranking as a third requisite of production' and .they called it capital. Man's contribution to wealth was-labeur,and they divided it into two heads—thedirect apckoation•st lab-our, and the accumulated result of past labour. Capital must begin by saving in the- sense- of postponing pre- sent enjoyment for future .aawntage. Be did not mean by saving, hoarding in the same- sense as a miser li-carded gold in. an old stocking. The use of captital enabled its 'saner to-wei4. and' this power of waiting was the key to success and industry. With regard to the law which governed the- productive power of land, without labour„ land would not pro- duce. This was not st.,-ietly true-because land produced fruits and berries long before maisever- commenced the I cultivation of land, but the quantity to be produced I depended upon the amount of labour and. capital ex- ; pended upon the land. 500 yearssago; England' was as • big as it is now and was-under equally favourable natural condi.ions, but there vaa-eight ti 1214P3 as much- produced from the land of England to-day as, was • prodhced from the same land 500 yearscago. This-was no doubt due to improved pn>ceases, to m increased amount of labour. There was a point when the increase oflabourupon the land would not result in aaproportional increase in pro- duce, and this was called the law- of dinaiiishing,neturns, which was founded upoic the lawoofi soientific• naming, lf it were not for ti-laiv, wo•shosid be able ter raise from one farm the, whole produce' reqpiked for England, but it woull ; need a great deal* of' capital and a great deal of labour,, and; there would be no fear of over-populition. The law, of diminishing returns applied not ono -agricultural land but in an increased degree to- the productiveness of mines. Malthus laid down a law that population had the- paver of increasing ranch faster than it had of supply- ing itself with food, and that the check was the difficulty ;of procuring a bare subsistante.• The Lecturer- pointed out how many things had occured of; which nalthus 'could not have foresaen,- and the most exact statement of the law of popution wtheti app:ied in England, would be this, that populatica was net much greater than it was by reasornofthe difficulty of procuringa sub- ' sistenee up to the standard of conaftrt set up by any particular class in aeciety. The standard of comfort varied very much ir.adifferert• countries and in afferent localities. In the South of ,Eogland it was rusign of extreme poverty vhea the alsildren went about in bare feet, but in the Northit was qiiite a eaannon thing,boots not being considered necessaries. The efficiency of tahaur depended upon the food el adabourer. Fbod was 'the fuel which droaothe haanau engine, and although an ' Indian Coolie lived upon rice; which-costs practically nothing, if a contractor wanted to; undertake heavy work, he woulO, find hotter to employ highly paid Europeans- than no • employ. Coolie labourers. The efficiency 4,;labou,i- danended upon the interest of the labourer •ia his v-crk, and upon the regularity and permanency. of the- employment. The latter was one of -thei grea..zst factors-in the efficiency of labour. The efficiency of labour alsodepended upon the mode in which it was orgingsed and' divided. Eighteen different workmen a wero• employed in the process of making pins. Adam ;Siaith caleakited that one man could only make two or three pinsu;day, whereas by the subdivision of labonr in, a small factory, they were able to turn out 5,C8‘0, pins :sr head.nor day, such was the economic advantage of aubdividertfdabour. There was a dark side to this subdivisiOn of labour. What must be the mental state ota raan -after- 20 years constant em- ployment in filial; keys.at•Wolvesimmpton ? What must be ihe chance of.such a man obtaining work again if he were throwuentotemploymenthunless he could fit into exactly the same place, ja exactly-the same trade? But there was brightness in, the-tbenght thatin time all those operaZiensreqeiting onaNe.reechanicall dexterity in repeating tae same operation over and ovceagain would be done by.enichine7 and the, work which, would be left to human . labour would be, that which required thought and judgraent. Iri, conclusion„, the lecturer pointed cut that there wasat counteracting law to the law c:ldiministalig returns-which he might call the law of aGreasing: returns cf human effort, and the- economic organisaiitia of labour, and this produced an increasing return Item labeur.—Mr. Huvnphreys,the hon. sec., said the Committee twil,done all they could to bring these lectures within the reach of the widest possible con- stituer.ep and I-Ad reduced' the price, to the nominal chargegand he -appealed to, those present' to divide the labour.; end laelpsthe Committee to dispose-of the tickets. The business of' paying the money was then proceeded with. MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. On Wednesday evening, Mrs. R. Garnett read a paper entitled "Travels in Greece," In spite of the turbulent state of the elements, there was a good attendance of members and others. The paper wsa highly interesting, touching as it d,tft upon the ancient history of the Greeks, and giving descrip- tions of the wonderful temples erected, in honour of the gods. Mrs. Garnett illustratod her paper by some very beautiful photoS of the temples at Athens; also a photograph of the costly statue of Miners "the martial maid," end soma specimens of clothing worn by the modern Greeks, and other relics from Athens and Corinth. Mr. R. Garuett supplemented by giving his impiession of modern Greece, which were not of a very sanguine nature for its future. Messrs, Aylward (Warrington), Car-. rick (Carlisle), .1. T. Gummersall and Dignikin spoke expressing thanks to Mrs. Garnett, whi.gh brought a very enjoyable evening t.oa clue,

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

DAMAGE TO PROPERTY IN WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, two lads, named Alfred Paley and Edward Elarroway, were charged with having done wilful damage to iron palisades belonging to Miss Gaskell, in Edward-st. It was stated that boys were in the habit of knocking the tops off the palisades with stones, and the two lads named had con- fessed to doing part of the damage. The Chairman (Alderman Davies) said complaints were made to magis- trates in the streets about the damage that was being done to property in Warrington. Each of the lads was ordered to pay ss. compensation. SHOCKING CONDUCT OF A SON. Thomas Conway was charged with having been drunk in Knutsford-road, also with assaulting his father, Patrick Conway. The father said that last week he buried his wife. Since then his son had been drinking. On Thursday he returned home almost every hour and asked tor money. Defendant got hold of him and dashed him against the sofa and wall. He had turned on him like a lion, and had threatened to take his life. Defend- ant was acting in so rough a manner on Thursday that he (complainant) was frightened of him and had to leave the house. Prisoner was committed to prison for two months, with hard labour and bound over to keep the peace for six months in one surety of £5, and himself in £lO, or in default one month's imprisonment. A SOLICITOR AND HIS POODLE DOG. At the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, Mr. W. H. .1. Jenkins. solicitor, was summoned for allowing his dog to wander at large unmuzzled. Sergeant Barnes was proceeding to state the facts,when the defendant rose and at once admitted the offence. He said he was sorry the police had had trouble with the dog, but it was not his fault. He thought the sergeant would agree with him that it was the fault of his housekeeper. It was a little pug dog, and it was almost impossible ta keep a muzzle on it, for its neck was bigger than its head, and if a muzzle was put on, the animal pulled it off with Its paws. He thought, however, the dog had always treated the police with great courtesy. (Laughter.)—Mr. Bleckly (chairman) said he had been in the same cir- cumstances himself, and had been fined, and he (Mr. Jenkins) would be fined Is. and costs. ASSAULT ON A WIFE. At the Warrington Police Court, on Friday, Daniel Mclntosh was summoned for assaulting his wife, Sarah Mclntosh, on the 11th inst.—Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for complainant, said he would ask the rnagis- trates to commit the defendant loran aggravated assault. The parties had been married 24 years; but some years ago complainant left her husband owing to his brutality. The woman was 77 years of age, and defendant was a little younger. On the day in question defendant re- turned home at midnight. He then began to assault his wife who had done or said nothing to mto cause such conduct. ?d Complainant had several bruises on her arm, being the effects of defendant's blows. The day after the assault the wife left him because she could not live with him any longer.—After hearing evidence on both sides the Bench considered it was not a case of aggra- vated assault, and ordered the defendant to pay 10s. costs, and be bound over in one surety of £5 to keep the peace towards his wife for six months. CHARGED ON SUSPICION. At the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, John Irlam and Rose Thompson, were charged with having in their possession a watch and chain, supposed to have been stolen.—P.C. Evans stated from information he received, at a quarter to one on Wednesday afternoon . he stopped the prisoners and said to them " You have a watch in your possession, and you will have to give an account as to where you got it from." Both prisoners denied the charge, whereupon the Constable said they I would have to go to the Police Station. Whilst taking them into custody he was met by Constable Monaghan in I Buttermarket-St., to whom the male defendant handed I over the watch, remarking that it did not belong to him I and that the woman had given it him to pawn. At the I Police Station the woman said she belonged to Liverpool and that she had had the watch presented to her by a man. The pendant was afterwards found on the woman. —The Chief Constable said he had written to Liverpool and Manchester respecting the prisoners, and he asked for a remand for 48 hours. This was granted. ASSAULT BY A FATHER. At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, John Cliff, labourer, was charged with haying been drunk in Cockhedge-lane, at nine o'clock, on Monday night ; also with assaulting his son Adam, aged 15, on the same evening. Prisoner pleaded guilty to the first offence, but denied the assault. P.C. :Turner deposed that shortly before nine o'clock on the day in question, he was in Buttermarket-St., when the boy Adam went up to him, and complained that his father had assaulted him. The lad was bleeding from the side of his neck, and witness asked what had caused the flow of blood. The boy re- plied that his father had done it by knocking him down and kicking him. Witness then proceeded in company with the boy, to Cockhed.ge-lane, where he saw a large crowd had assembled. He then said to the boy, "Now, you go on, and if your father again assaults you, I will come to your assistance." The boy immediately ap- proached his father, who instantly cot hold of him, and struck him. Witness then took the prisoner into custody. Adam Cliff corroborated the statement of the constable. Prisoner said he was irritated with his son refusing to go home. A fine of 10s. and costs was im- posed, or the alternative of 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: POLICEMAN USES HIS STAFF.
div.p: A POLICEMAN USES HIS STAFF.

At the Warrington Borough Court on Monday the Chief Constable explained the circumstances under which a Warrington policeman may use his baton. The case was one in which James Hennessy was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Town-hill on Sunday night and assaulting Constable Clough. The Chief Con- stable said a brother of the prisoner, who is well known to the magistrates, was acting in an indecent manner, when the constable remonstrated with him for doing so. The man followed the officer and struck him on the back. The constable was then attempting to take him into custody when the prisoner, James Hennessey, came up and kicked him severely. The officer then turned his attention to this new assailant, and there being a good deal of resistance called upon the landlord of the Boar's Head to render him assistance. A crowd had assembled, and a chair was thrown out of one of the houses and it struck the officer. Other articles of furniture were thrown at him, and "a sad melee took place." The officer, in self-defence, drew his staff and struck the prisoner on the head with it, causing a wound. He wished to explain that whenever a policeman drew his staff, he was required to report that fact, and all thE. circumstances connected with it, to the police office. A Warrington policeman, however, rarely made use of his staff. He had a perfect right to do so when alone, and when it was necessary either to secure a prisoner or to preserve the peace. It was very possible that had an older constable been on duty at the place in question he might not have said anything about the indecency, as Michael Hennessey (prisoner's brother, who was the cause of the disturbance) was drunk. He was inclined tothink there had been a little hastiness all round. Eviclonce in sup- port of the Chief Constalle's statemeot was then given and it also transpired that the officer had to take refuge in a public-house owing to the attentions of the crowd, who were anxious to effect the release of the prisoner. Alderman Davies said that had not this been the prisoner's first appearance he would have been sent to gaol without the option of a fine. He would be fined 20s. and costs.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY. Before Alderman Burgess, Alderma Chandley, and Mr. R. Garnett. STEALING A RABBIT.—Three lads, named J. Leonardy (14), P. Hanlon (13), and T. Armitage (13), were charged with stealing a tame rabbit, value 35., the pro- perty of John Stannistreet, from 84, Battersby-lane, on Monday last. The defendants, it appeared, sold the rab- bit to a dealer for 25., and divided the money. Armit- age and Hanlon were each committed for 14 days, and ordered on the expiration of the sentence to be sent to a reformatory for three years. Leonardy was ordered to receive 12 strokes of the birch rod, and be detained in custody until six o'clock in the evening. ASSAULTING A WlFE.—Edward Tinckler, a Ship Canal navvy, was brought up on a warrant charged with as- saulting his wife, Ellen, on the 9th October. P.C. Critchley proved arresting the prisoner. The complain- ant said that on the day in question, when she asked her husband for some money, he struck and kicked her, and, brandishing a knife, threatened "what he would do for her." The prisoner was bound over in his own surety for £lO and another of £lO, to keep the peace for six months, or in default to go to prison for a month. ALLEGED NECILECT OF FAmrLy.—Thornas Smith was charged with refusing to maintain his wife and family, who had become chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—Mr. Basil Shearer prosecuted on behalf of the Guardians. He said the case first came before them on the 10th September, when he (Mr. Shearer) tried to arrange matters between the defend- ant and his wife. He ref Ted to do anything for hers and the case went on until the 30th September, when she was admitted to the workhouse. Mr. Harbourne, relieving officer, saw the defendant, but could not do anything with him. He (Mr. Shearer) thought that Smith ought to be compelled to come to some arrange- ment with his wife.—Mr Browne, who represented the defendant, contended that his client was not liable. Smith and his wife had lived an unhappy life for three or four years, owing to the wife giving way to drink. She had sold some hair-seated chairs, the children's cloth ing, her husband's boots, and other articles. When they lived together Smith gave his wife £1 a week out of the 235. he earned. He had asked his wife to live with him, and after that, Mr. Browns contended, he was justified in refusing to maintain her. He would, however, main- tain his children, but not his wife, because she was in good employment.—Inspector Cox said that defendant complained to him about six months ago, and in the presence of witness asked his wife to go and live with him again. They each accused the other of drinking.— Mr. Warburton said that the defendant was a sober and steady man.—The Bench decided to withdraw the sum- mons on the defendant promising to contribute 2s. ed. weekly to the youngest child's support. He was to have tbe custody of the other three children.

WARRINGTON v. LEIGH.

Since the withdrawal of Warrington from the West Lancashire Rugby Union League, the inter- est in the few matches arranged with the several clubs who help to form the above union has some- what abated as was instanced on Saturday, when not more than 200 to 250 people accompanied the Warringtonians to Leigh. The Leigh people, however, mustered strongly, and there would not be less than four thousand people present when the kick off was effected. The recent accidents to several Warringtonians prevented them placing their best team in the field, but still a representative fifteen did duty. Leigh made a special whip for the occasion, amongstthetn being Graham, late of Kendal Hornets.

Coop kicked off against wind and sun, and Thorniley's burly form charging the kick off, Berry improved the visitor's position by a dribble past the quarter flag. A pass from Barnes to Lawless found play near the Leigh posts, where Antrobas essayed to get is, Rowe pulling him up. A free kick to Leigh followed, and a clever piece of work by R. McMaster transferred the game to neutral ground, but it only remained there a short time, the superior back play of Warrington easily staving off the attack ; in fact, Leigh never passed the centre flag again this half. Off-side tactics by Leigh gave Evans a free kick, and Warrington missed a rare chance when Coop failed in his endeavours to clear. Sterling forward play by Turner, Dutton, Thorniley, and Jolley kept the homesters strictly on the defensive, and a flue run and pass by Antrobus to Lawless gave the latter a good chance, but he knocked the oval on. War- rington continued to have the best of it, and after Coop had relieved his lines in brilliant style, Antrobus again got away, and passing to Barnes the last-named threw to Lawless, who made no mistake this time, a try being the result. Barnes took the easy place kick, and, singular o state, missed it. Bandies met the kick off, and Nevins, Turner,and Jolley showed up in tackling and running. Coop was equal to the task set him, and with less experienced hands in this responsible position, the Warringtonians must have scored. The Leigh men too knew the sterling work of their custodian,. for . .

repeatedly they passed to him when pressed back on their line. A fine piece of play by the home back was followed by another passing movement by Antrobus and Barnes, the last-named being thrown into touch a yard from the line. Boscow next essayed a drop at goal, and a minor was recorded. Evans now had a turn, and was found to be as bold an obstacle as ever. A capital kick by the Warrington threequarter caused Coop some anxiety, but he luckily cleared, only to see Boscow returning as cleverly. Bate threw to Barnes, who transferred to Evans, Smith spoiling the movement by grassing the latter before he could get clear. A fine dribble by the Warrington forwards, foremost amongst whom were Berry, Jolley, and Bandies, was staved off by Coon, and Evans now made the run of the day. Starting from the half way he ran through the thick of his opponents, being held on the line by three Leighites clinging to him. A minor followed this brilliant run, and half-time was then called, Warrington 0-1-2, Leigh nil. On resuming, play at the onset was confined to neutral ground. Smart saving tactics by Nevins checked some strong rushes of the heavy Leigh forwards. Useful kicks by Coop forced Warrington to defend, and exchanges by the opposing backs found the game hovering near the visitors' posts. Thorniley. Nevins, and Beard were foremost ma dribble, but unfortunately the latter got hurt at this juncture of the game, which necessitated his removal to Liverpool. The Warrington forwards now became a trifle disc:a.. ganized, and the homesters using their weight to advan- tage, and tackling severely, compelled the game to be con- tested at the Warrington quarters. The game was chiefly confined to the forward, it being one continual series of scrimmages and line-outs. A free kick by Lawson gave Coop a chance for a shot at goal, which went outside by about a foot, and towards the close Higgins notched a try, which Coop failed to augment. Jolley and Turner made a futile bid in the last minute of the game to regain the lead, and the whistle brought a welcome relief, the game remaining drawn, the final score reading—War- rington, 0-1-2 ; Leigh, 0-1-1. Warrington: J. Boscow, back; J. W. Evans, T. Barnes, and P. H. Lawless, three- quarter backs ; J. T. Bate and W. Antrobus (captain), half backs; Fair Turner, J. Jolley, W. Bandies, W. Nevins, G. Beard, B. Berry, J. T. Thorni ley, J. Holmes, and E. Dillon, forward. Leigh: Coop, back; Forrest, Smith, and Coffee, three-quarter backs; Shovelton and Rowe, half backs; Lawson, Gregory, Taylor, Graham, R. McMaster, W. McMaster, Jackson, Higgins, and Knowles, forwards. Referee, Mr. Vickers, Salford.
