WIDNES V. MANCHESTER RANGERS (A) TEAMS.—Widnes (A) met Manchester Rangers (A) at the former place on Saturday afternoon. From the first the homesters had the best of the game. Tries were obtained for Widnes by Holt, Morris, and Burgess, one of these being converted by Morris. The combination shown by Widnes was excellent. The visitors also played a good game. Final result :—Widnes, 1 goal, 3 tries, 4 minors; Manchester Rangers, 1 minor.

EAST CITESIZIRE T. WEST CHESHIRE.—The first of the county fixtures the trial game, was played off on Satur- day, at Stockport, in the presence of a large body of spectators. The teams were as follows :—West Cheshire : S. Houghton (Runcorn), back; T. Davies (Runcorn), Watson (Birkenhead Wanderers), and R. de C. Steele (Birkenhead Park) three-quarter backs; W. E. Evans and S. Abrams (Runcorn), halfbacks; W. Faulkner, I'. Riley, R. Dolan. J. Gayter, W. Rigby (Runcorn), P. H. Lockwood, T. W. Lockwood *(Birkenhead Park), R. B. Eskrigge, W. A. Williams (New Brighton), and G.Garner (Birkenhead Wanderers), forwards. East Cheshire: J. T. Haslam (Dukenfield), back; Harvey (Sale), Ogden (Stockport), and Cookson (Sale), three-quarter backs; Thorpe (Sale) and Naylor (Stockport), half backs; ' Walton, Stephens (Sale), Birch, Lewis, (Wilmslow), R. Morton (A.ltrincham), S. Hague (Dukinfield), J.Schofield, Potts, Dr. Smith, and Dain (Stockport) forwards. The West, winning the toss, kicked off, and Scho- field rushed the oval to the West 25, where Dolan saved neatly. and Cookson mulling a pass the West forwards forced Murray. Dain and Naylor did useful work. The East were attacking their opponents' line, when one of the West forwards executed a beautiful dribble, only to be repulsed by Schofield and E. Harvey_ .Thorp and Cookson again endangered the West line, and Cookson, after a grand dodgy run, passed to Harvey, he getting over. Murray failed at goal. The Easterners pressed, Ogden and Schofield being very notice- able ; and immediately afterwards Dr. Smith got over the line, Potts kicking at goal. Watson, after a good combination by the West forwards, registered a try, no goal resulting. At half time the result was East Cheshire one goal, one try, one minor ; West Cheshire one try. On change of ends Thorpe and earvey were conspicuous and Ogden did grand work for East. By good combina- tion the leather was taken to East quarters, Murray re- lieving finely. Gavter and Murray exchanged kicks. Thorpe was applauded for dribbling, Ogden and Naylor on the one hand, and Abraham, Houghton, and Taylor on the other, displayed grand form. Final result : East Cheshire, one goal, one try ; West Cheshire, two tries.

WIDNES v. MANCHESTER RANGERS.—This fixture was decided at Manchester on Saturday, before about 1,000 spectators. J. Smith for Widnes kicked off, and some good play amongst the Widnes forwards, early made the Rangers resort to defensive tactics. Some nice play by the home team transferred operations to the visitors' 25, when Okell almost got in, Hartles and Clarke defending grandly. From a scrimmage, Okell again got possession, and made a very good drop at goal, the ball just going outside the posts, a minor only resulting. From the drop out, Widnes invaded the home territory, and kept play there for some time, hut were prevented from scoring by the plucky play of Okell. A. Hamnett was next prominent with a good run, but was stopped when on the line. From a scrimmage, H. Hasleham "(Tossed the line, the kick at goal by Hill being successful. On recommencing, the Widnes forwards rushed the ball down to the home line, where from a throw in on the line, Whelan got possession, and made a clean pass to Gordon, who grounded the leather, but the kick at goal by Barber failed. Widnes, encouraged by this result of their dashing play, commenced another attack, and Drummond and Clarke had hard lines. The visitors continued to press, and made matters very lively for the home backs, and subsequently Farmer crossed the line and scored what appeared to be a fair try, but the point was disallowed by the referee. At half time the score was Manchester Rangers one goal and two minors to Widnes one try. On changing ends Mee re- started for the home sido. a free kick falling to Laws soon after. A. Hamnett next made a futile attempt at a drop for goal, a minor being the result. The game at this period was very fast, the ball travelling rapidly from end to end. From a dribble by Whelan, the Widnes line was broken by FL Haslehatn, Who got away and scored the second try. Hill this time failed at goal. After the drop out, the Rangers paid a short visit to the Widnes quarters, but by good forward play the oval reached the centre again, and Widnes ex- perienced very hard lines. Score—Manchester Rangers, 1 goal, 1 try, and 3 minors, to Widnes 1 try and 1 minor. Teams :—Manchester Rangers : D. Hill, back ; A. Hamnett, H. Radcliffe, and T. Okell, three-quarter backs ; M. Borg and S. Taylor, half backs ; Herbert Hasleham, G. Pollard, E. Mee, H. Hasleham, W. Storer, W. Pearson, U. Ihbotson, R. Hamnett, and T. West- brook, forwards. Widnes: J. Hartles, back; J. Clarke, D. Brennan, and H. Peters, three-quarter backs ; H. Bar- ber and J. Drummond, half backs ; J. H. Smith, H. Hewitt, E. Gordon, J. Pearson, H. Farmer, P. Tickle, J. Whelan, Carroll, and Laws, forwards. WARRINGTON A. V. LEIGH A.—This match was played on the Wilderspool ground on Saturday, before a moder- ate number of onlookers. Isherwood started the game, and a decided attack was at once made on the visitors' goal, a minor being conceded. Following the drop out play still hovered about the vicinity of the Leigh 25, chiefly through the exertions of Knowles, Woods, Isher- wood, and Flackett,till Eceford kicked cleverly out of danger. Gradually Leigh wore the attacking party back, and when danger looked threatening, Webster cleared by a grand kick, and took warfare to his antagonists' stronghold. Unfortunately at this period the visitors' custodian injured his knee, and had to re- tire. Continuing, a free kick to Leigh was a welcome relief, taking play to the home quarters, where Lawless came round a scrimmage in fine style to midfield. Rus- sell, Molyneux, Barnes, and Catterall improved matters, but Officier intercepting a pass dashed away to Warring- ton territory and enabled his comrades to rush to within a few yards of the goal. The game was not allowed to remain here long, for a capital piece of play by Bate and Molyneux transferred matters to more desirable quarters Some fast forward play, in which Welsby. Knowles, Russell and Barnes were notable, took the leather fur- ther into Leigh lines, and after a spell of lively passing Catterall scored, which Webster improved. After a bout of even tactics, Webster gave a taste of his abilities by dashing through his opponents, and a wide pass from Mather enabled Daniels to run in a capital try, whilst immediately afterwards the same player secured a simi- lar try after passing by Lawless and Mather. In no wise disheartened by these reverses the visitors played up pluckily, and for a time succeeded in holding their own, until some grand transfers between Lawless, who throughout showed vast improvement, Bate, and Web- ster, and another strong rush by the latter, pressed Leigh sorely. A flying kick by Collier gave temporary relief, but ultimately Lawless and Mather passed splendidly, and handing over to Bate, he, by one of his inimitable runs, obtained a try. Further grand passing by the home backs ensued, and Knowles, Hackett, Welsby, and Isherwood dribbled close to the line, and from a rush by Woods, Catterall scored, the same player securing another good try directly afterwards, the half-time score reading Warrington 1-5-0 to nil. Resuming, the visiting for- wards, headed by Lawson and Clarke, rushed into their opponents' territory, but Daniels and Bate speedily worked the ball back again. A most sensational run by Webster clean through his opponents was frantically cheered, and from a pass by Mather, Daniels dodged over splendidly at the corner flag, whilst he again repeated the dose from a t?-I;kv piece of work a few minutes after- wards. Succeeding this a rattling dribble by Phcenix, Edwards, an(' Sutton took took the game well into War- rington stronghold, but Barnesand Catterall by some fast play completely altered affairs, and forced Leigh to act strictly on the defensive. At length Leigh cleared and assumed a threatening attitude, until Bate saved twice in daring fashion. Again the home team attacked, and from some passing Russell ran over. Webster convert- ing from near touch. The kick-out was followed by a splendid rush of the visiting forwards, and for a time the game continued of an even character. Eventually a grand bit of passing by Lawless, Mather, Daniels, Bate, and Webster resulted in a try, and Woods forced a minor by a strong run. After this, Welsby was prominent by a good piece of play, and Sampson getting the oval, gal- loped close to the line, and being spun into touch, bounced the. ball and ran over. Three grand tries fol- lowed in quick succession to Webster's credit, all the result of passing, the last being obtained behind the posts, which he converted, leaving Warrington winners by 3-11-2 to nil. Teams :—Warrington: Sampson, back; Webster, Bate, and Daniels, three-quarters; Mather and Lawless, half backs; Isherwood, Molyneaux, Knowles, Russell, Hackett, Welsby, Woods, Catterall, and Barnes, forwards. Leigh : Eceford, back; Brisco, Collier and Unsworth, threequarters ; °Meier and }knocks. half

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL-RUGBY.

In Lancashire Rugby circles the meeting of Swinton and Salford is a specially interesting event. Why it should be so it is hard to say, for Swinton generally beats Salford with greater ease than it beats some other Lancashire teams. Saturday's game was no exception to the rule, for the Salfordians had to submit to a de- feat by a goal and a try to a minor. If Swinton had not had hard luck probably their majority would have been larger.

Yorkshire is the county for big gates at Rugby matches. There were about 10,000 spectators on Satur- day, to see Hull beaten by Huddersfield, and 8,000 had the pleasure, or displeasure, as the case might be, of see- ing Bradford upset Halifax by three goats to n)thing. Among Yorkshire teams Wakefield Trinity seem to be in a rather uncertain condition just now, as Batley beat them on their own ground last week.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

All the twelve Lea-g-U-e--cia;-v-ire busily engaged on Saturday. The champions paid a visit to Accrington, and wound up with a victory of three goals to ono. The Reds are having a very bad time of it, and have still to ' score their first success The play of the North End left little to be desired, the forwards working together har- moniously and the defence being very sound, despite the absence of Howarth. Everton had their winning career checked at Perry Barr, where the best they could do was to make a draw with Aston Villa. Right up to the close defeat seemed likely for the Liverpool men, but they drew level just before time expired. There was some capital football, the match being the best seen on the Birmingham ground this season.

Wolverhampton Wanderers were far too clever for Derby County, and now share the honours of first place with Everton. , As the latter, however, have played only six matches as against the " Wolves " seven, they have a slightly better average. Bolton Wanderers came off with flying colours at Burnley, where they won an excellent contest by two goals to one. West Bromwich Albion had the worst of the luck at Nottingham, where the verdict was against them by three goals to two. Blackburn Rovers were successful against Sunderland by a like margin, Gow, of the suspended Renton team, keeping goal for the cup-holders for the first time.

The Alliance furnished a big surprise in the shape of the defeat of Newton Heath at Bootle by five goals to nothing. The visiting forwards were terribly weak and halting. Stoke are now at the head of the Alliance list, with Notts Forest second.

Over the border a sensation was created by the third Lanark knocking the famous Queen's Park out of the Glasgow Cup competition. The honours of the Scottish League still rests with Dumbarton, who are three points in front of Glasgow Rangers.

MISCELLANEOUS. An American telegram says that the amatuer cham- pionship sports held at Analska Island on Saturday, John Owen, of Detroit, compassed 100 yards in 94secs. In the broad jump competition, F. Copeland of the Manhattan Club, cleared 23ft. 3iin. Queckburner, also of the Man- hattan Club, threw the 561 b weight a distance of 321 t. 10in. Owen's fine performance, if well attested, eclipses all accredited amateur times for 100 yards, whether made in America, England, or Australia. Several years ago, Ritchie, of Bradford, was credited with doing 91sec., at Aston Lower Grounds, Birmingham; but the track being a sloping one, the performance was not accepted as a record. Wharton covered the distance in 10sec., at London, in July, 1886.

div.head: SHIPPING DISASTERS.
div.p: SHIPPING DISASTERS.
COLLISION OFF CARDIFF.--STEAMER MISSING
The steamer Patterdale, of Newca.stle-on-Tyne, arrived at Cardiff on Wednesday morning, having apparently been in collision with an unknown steamer, which is mis- sing.
THE DROWNING OF TWO SAILORS.

FREIDRICHSTADT, WEDNESDAY.—The two British sailors who were drowned while attempting to swim aboard their ship as she was leaving the harbour on the 13th Inst. belonged to the crew of the three-masted schooner Ocean Spray. THE WRECK OF A LIVERPOOL BARQUE. • •

HALIFAX, WEDNESDAY.—The four sailors left on the wreck of the barque Melmerby have now been rescued. The gale on the Nova Scotian coast has proved very destructive, twelve vessels having been lost off Cape Breton.

div.head: LABOUR AND CAPITAL
div.p: LABOUR AND CAPITAL
Seven hundred plush and velvet weavers in the em- ploy of Messrs. Lister and Co., Bradford, struck work on Tuesday, in support of a demand by the cutters for an advance of three shillings per week.
A PERMANENT STAFF.

Some corn porters, engaged on Messrs. Allan's ship Grecian, in the Albert Docks, London, struck again on Monday, for an advance of wages. The London and India Docks Joint Committee have decided to engage a permanent staff of labourers at 24.5. weekly, to cope with any emergency. THE AUSTRALIAN STRIKES.

It is expected that the New South Wales Railway em- ployes will refuse to handle coal from Bulli. Free labourers are numerous at Newcastle, and six coal trains have arrived there. Tranquillity prevails at Bulli. The stevedores and labourers at Melbourne have decided to resume work pending the result of the Conference be- tween the employers and workmen.

div.head: SCOTCH IRON TRADE DISPUTE.
div.p: THE SCOTCH IRON TRADE DISPUTE.

Eight days have now passed since the blowing out of the furnaces, and the dispute in the Scotch iron trade is apparently as far from a settlement as ever. The men adhere to their demands, and the masters refuse even to discuss them. From Kilbirme it is reported that a large consignment of pig iron arrived from the North of Eng- land, on Saturday, for the Glengarnock Steelworks. The consignment consisted of 103 wagons, with about 700 tons.

div.head: TERRIBLE HOTEL FIRE IN AMERICA.
div.p: TERRIBLE HOTEL FIRE IN AMERICA.
DISTRESSING LOSS OF LIFE. £lOO,OOO DAMAGE.

NEW Yorix,TEIIIRSDAY.—The Leland Hotel at Syracuse, the largest Hotel in Central New York, was destroyed by fire last midnight. The catastrope was attended by some terrible scenes. In one instance a woman was being lowered from a window by a rope when a burning windowsill severed the line, and the unfortunate woman fell a shapekss mass upon the pavement below. Many persons crazed with fright jumped from windows, and were dashed to pieces in the street. One woman was found nursing her baby crouching on a stairway, both being overcome by smoke. The loss to property is estimated at £lOO,OOO. LATER.—Another despatch from Syracuse gives fur- ther harrowing details of the fire at the Leland Hotel. One particularly affecting scene was witnessed. A man and his wife were seen at a window on the fifth storey, where rescue was impossible. The woman showed a disposition to jump into the street below, but her hus- band was seen to be entreating her not to do so. The crowd assembled outside were immediately afterwards horror-stricken to see both husband and wife suddenly disappear enveloped in flames. Other similar tragedies were witnessed. Many persons jumped half naked from upper floors on to some sheds, and re- ceived severe injuries. One of the most fright- ful incidents in connection with the disaster was the death of a woman who leaped from the fifth storey. The police were prepared with nets to catch those who made the terrible leap. A man and a woman first jumped at almost the same moment into the net, and escaped with broken limbs. The next person, how- ever, who leaped was a woman dressed in her night attire, and missing the net, she fell with a terrible crash on the pavement. The injured were removed as soon as possible to houses close by, the police stations being con- verted into temporary hospitals. NEW YORK, THURSDAY NooN.—Although no exact in- formation as to the number of nersons who lost their lives in the fire at Syracuse has yet been obtained, the latest estimate places the mortality at much less than the num- ber at first fixed by those who witnessed the disaster. It is now believed that only three of the visitors and five servants perished, but nearly thirty others were seriously injured.

div.head: ST. HELENS LADY AND THE MYSTERIOUS PARCEL.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS LADY AND THE MYSTERIOUS PARCEL.

On Saturday afternoon a young St. Helens lady paid a visit to Liverpool, in company with a male friend, and after visiting one of the drapery establishments for which the city is so famous, she returned to Lime-st. Station and deposited in the cloakroom a small brown paper parcel, which contairien several yards of cretonne. The couple then went to "look round" the city, and on reaching Lime-st. in time to catch the 10.50 train to St. Helens, Ma% took the ticket, and presenting it at the cloakroom window received what he then believed to be the parcel deposited by the young lady earlier in the day. The parcel was placed in the carriage and duly carried to the home of the young lady in Duke-st., St. Helens. When she came to look at the exterior of the parcel she became apprehensive that there was something wrong, and OD taking the brown paper partially off she came upon an old Liverpool newpaper dated 1888. This being removed, a dirty cotton pocket handkerchief was exposed to view. Too disgusted to proceed further, she dropped the parcel on the floor, and, .rumour says, gave it a hearty kick, and sent it flying into a corner. A little later, the parcel was again looked at, and a coloured union shirt,like those I worn by sailors, became the next object of observation, and no little add!tion 11 disgust. This, however, soon gave way to surprise, for in the centre she found three small leather bags, two of which contained twenty sove- reigns each and the other contained ten sovereigns. With commendable promptitude the young lady informed Chief- constable Wood., and that gentleman at once placed him- self in communication with the Lime-st. Station officials. Inquiries were made on Tuesday afternoon, and the £5O and the mysterious wrapper reached Lime-st. Station, and the parcel belonging to the young lady was despatched to her at St. Helens. It is not too much to hope that the conduct of the young lady will not go unrewarded. It does not appear to be definitely known at Lime-st. when the parcel was deposited, nor was any declaration made as to the value it contained. Whatever was its origin it had lain in the cloakroom unclaimed for some time, and but for the mistake of the clerk it might bave been transferred to the racks of the missing luggage stores, there to be dealt with in the ordinary way. EXTRAORDINARY SEQUEL. On Thursday, at the Liverpool Police Court, before Mr. Raffles, a respectably dressed youth, named William Beer, 17 years of age, was charged with having stolen upwards of £5O, the money of his employer, Mr. Benussi, pawnbroker, Paradise-st. Detective sub-inspector Grubb gave the details of the finding of the parcel as narrated above. He said the matter was put into the hands of Detective-Inspector Atkins, who from marks on the parcel suspected the prisoner, and at once went to Mr. Benussi's shop. He and Detective Waring, of the city force, had an interview with the prisoner, and after some hesitation he admitted that the writing on the paper was his, and that he had taken the money from his employer. He was then taken into custody by Constable Wareing. Evidence was given by Atkins and Wareing in corroboration of Grubb's statement. It was also stated that the parcel was deposited at Lime-st. Station on the 6th of October. Mr. Benussi stated that he did not wish the prisoner to be severely dealt with. The prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge, and was sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour. On hear- ing his sentence Beer remarked that it would kill his mother.
The spinning mill of Mr. Lee, of Mosesgate, near Bol- ton, was on Thursday destroyed by fire. The workpecple escaped with the loss of their outdoor garments. The damage is estimated at £20,000.

GENERAL Satisfaction commands the vast army of people who use " SUNLIGHT SOAY."—Advt. A Vienna telegram states that the Turkish soldiers and police have perpetrated many cruel atrocities on Armenian prisoners. Torture has been freely resorted to, with lamentable results. In Armenia the authorities continue to distribute arms to the Turks, and the Armenians are robbed and murdered with impunity. The jewels stolen from Lord Henry Somerset's Surrey residence, Reigate Priory, where the Marchioness of Anglesey is staying, include some valuable rings, brooches, and the Marchioness of Anglesey's gold watch and chain. There is no clue to the thieves. At Bow-st. on Thursday, Henry Ives, recently a tele- graph operator, was committed for trial, charged with attempting to defraud a publicaan named Pratt of £43 by means of forged telegrams. It is alleged that pri- soner, being in collusion with some post-office clerks, got the winning horses' names inserted in betting telegrams handed in before the race was run. div.head: ECCLES DIVISION ELECTION.
div.p: THE ECCLES DIVISION ELECTION.

The writ for the election of a member for the Eccles division has been issued, and on Saturday it was arranged that the nominations should be received on Thursday last, and that the election should take place on the 22nd inst. A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Roby was held at Irlam on Saturday night. The candidate discussed Lord Salisbury's foreign policy. A resolution in favour of his candidature was carried unani- mously. Meetings in support of Mr. Egerton's candita- ture were held at Roe Green and Patricroft, Sir John Gorst, M. P., Sir W. H. Houldsworth, M. P., and Mr. W. E. Macartney4l. P., being among the speakers. The Hon. Algernon Fulke Egerton, Conservative, and Mr. Henry J. Roby, Gladstonian Liberal, were on Thurs- day nominated as candidates for the vacancy in the Eccles division. The polling will take place next Wed nes-

day. On Wednesday night Mr. Roby's candidature was supported by a public meeting at Walkden, where the speakers included Mr. R. Neville, M.P., Mr. H. Harrison, M.P., and Mr. Clancy,M.P. At a meeting held on Wed- nesday night at Irlams-o'-th'-Height in support of the Liberal candidate the principal speakers were Mr. Ver- non K. Armitage and Mr. P. J. Power, M.P., Mr. Carson, Q.C., and Mr. Ashmead Bartlett were the principal speakers at a meeting of Mr. Egerton's supporters held in the Eccles Town Hall. A meeting at Winton in sup- port of Mr. Egerton's candidature was addressed by Mr. Jasper More, M.P. Posters have been issued in the Eccles Division appeal- ing for support on Mr. Roby's behalf as a supporter of the Eight Hours Bill for miners, free education, reform of the House of Lords, justice to Ireland, local option, Sunday closing, and retention of the common lands for the people.

div.head: LITE SUPERINTENDENT WEIR.
div.p: THE LITE SUPERINTENDENT WEIR.

Before the ordinary business of the court was corn- I menced on Saturday at Ne-vton Sessions, the acting- chairman of the Bench, Mr. T. J. Gillespie, said that he had to refer with the deepest regret to the said and sud- den death of Supt. Weir, who, for the past five years, had taken such a prominent part in the business of that court. It was difficult to realize that only four weeks ago Suot. Weir was sitting in his usual place there, the very picture of health, and with apparently a long and useful life before him. He was a most energetic and hard-working officer, and it had been stated to him (Mr. Gillespie) that the disease which carried Supt. Weir off so suddenly was the result of overwork and over-anxiety regarding that work. In the many difficult and often painful duties he was celled upon to perform he always carried them out with firmness and exactitude ; but so genial in manner was he, and of such kindness of heart, that he was respected and esteemed by all with whom he came in contact. He was a man who would be sadly. missed, and their deepest sympathy was with his widow and children in this their sad bereavement.

Mr. R. Stuart, on behalf of the legal profession, said he had the pleasure of knowing Supt. Weir for many years, and he entirely concurred in what had fallen from the Bench with reference to the late superintendent's un- failing kindness and courtesy. Mr. H. J. Longton also bore testimony to Supt. Weir's devotion to duty. Supt. Brassington (Wigan), who was much affected, said he felt that he had lost not only a brother officer, but a sincere and true friend of 14 or 15 years' standing.
FIRE IN LONDON.

div.head: EIGHT PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH, AND 13
div.p: EIGHT PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH, AND 13
INJURED.

_ A terrible fire broke out on Monday in the city of London at Messrs. Rowley and Brook's hat manufactory, Middle-st., Cloth Fair, Smithfield, London. resulting in eight deaths, and serious injury to thirteen other persons. The outbreak occurred shortly before one o'clock, and there were at the time about thirty people in the building. The first things noticed by outsiders were flames issuing from the upper storeys and persons appearing at the windows shouting and making frantic gesticulations for help. An alarm was promptly con- veyed to the local fire stations, and engines and escapes were soon on the scene. In the meantime,, however, a young man, named France, an employe, stood on a ledge on the ground floor window, and assisted several persons down from the storey above. He ultimately was com- pelled by the flames to jump to the ground. The occu- pants of the upper floor then tied some sheeting together, and by this means let down some of the women, eight or ten in number; but in one or two cases the sheeting gave way, and severe injuries were taused by the fall on the pavement. The flames spread with extraordinary rapidity, and the firemen, after effecting several more rescues with escapes, were obliged to desist, and pour water into the building. After half an boor the fire was got under. A young man named Charles J. Housman died on Tuesday from injurie3 received in the fire. Some others t remain in the hospital in a critical_ condition.

div.head: INQUEST. . .
div.p: THE INQUEST. . .

The inquest on the bodies of the eight persons who perished by the terrible fire last Monday, was opened on Thursday. Mr. Crawford, solicitor, representing the Common Council, said if his instructions were correct, there had been a serious infringement of the Petroleum Act. Mr. Filler, for Messrs. Rowley and Brooks, how- ever, replied that his clients were prepared to resist any proceedings that might be taken. Superintendent Hutchins deposed to the firemen arriving son after the outbreak. The flames spread so rapidly that it was use- less endeavouring to enter the building to save the in- mates. When the fire was subdued he entered, and found four women on the second floor, very much charred, and death appeared to have been from suffoca- tion. There was no delay in sendingfire escapes. Mr. R. S. Brook said about 25 gallons of naptha was taken in- to the basement half-an-hour before the outbreak oc- curred. There were no gas burners in the basement. The foreman always enjoined upon the workpeople the necessity of using naptha with care,but no printed regu- lations were circulated. The fire insurance office had seen naptha in the cellar, and passed it without remark. The inquiry was subsequently adjourned until Tues- day.

div.head: DEBASING ADVERTISEMENTS.
div.p: DEBASING ADVERTISEMENTS.

Sir,—You and your readers will be pleased to hear, that, I thanks to the press, not only has the audacious adver- tisement on the rocks of the Great Orme's Head been removed, but I am assured by official communications from Llandudno that such debasing advertisements will never again be permitted. This result is highly satisfac- tory. If the press will still further aid me, I hope to be able to prevent some further contemplated desecrations of this grand old mountain. Every foot of ground on the Great Orme is sacred. Tc profane and desecrate it, is sacrilege.—Yours truly, TRACY TURNERELLI.

Leamington, Oct. 13th. P.S.—To forwa.rd this good purpose, I am writing for gratuitous circulation some tracts on the Great Orme's Head. They will be sent, free of all cost, to all your readers who apply for them.

div.head: STANDING TO CLERGY.
div.p: STANDING TO CLERGY.

Sir,—This custom recently introduced in Runcorn Parish Church is causing some unpleasantness. It certainly may suit a pompous ritual such as the Romish Church, but is not certainly scriptural. Solomon wrote, "The rich and the poor meet together; the Lord is the maker of them all." Moses, Daniel, Peter, Jude, Paul and even Christ looked upon themselves as servants, brethren, not to lord it over the laity. "Oh, but," say these would-be priests," we are your lords; you must pay us and the choir homage when we proceed to or from the holy of house" (chancel). The chief office of an apostle was to preach. As Calvin remarks, "It hence appears what just objects of ridicule are those dumb dogs, who render themselves conspicuous only by their mitre and their crook, (alb, cope, stole, chasuble, mass vestments) and boast themselves to belthe successors of the Apostles.' Many parsons ignore the fact that the laity are their equals and often their superiors in learning ; that the word priest is not to be found in the christian ministry; and that in the early church laymen officiated. Bishop Ryle truly said the other week, "the clergy push out the laity," or as it been said in Runcorn they (laity) must listen to what is said; yes, but these ministers dare not say their trash from a public phtform, and give their hearers a chance of replying. How long will John Bull put up with their Runcorn, October 14th, 1890.
FALSE TEACHING.

div.head: "LIBERAL RE-UNION."-THE ECCLES ELECTION.
div.p: "LIBERAL RE-UNION."-THE ECCLES ELECTION.

Sir,—At no period since 1866 as at the present has the perfect re-union of the Liberal party been so capable of speedy accomplishment. Allow me through your gener- ous columns to remind all sincere dissentient Liberals (1) That true Liberal progress can never be attained by Tory Legislation (see Mr. Courtney M.P.'s recent speech). (2). That it is an intolerable disgrace that an important sec- tion of the British Empire immediately adjacent to its very centre still remains discontented and with bitter grievances unredressed. (3). That a policy of coercion has never reconciled an oppressed people but almost in- variably led to seperation—to wit, Belgium from Holland Schleswig Holstein from Denmark, the United States, from Great Britain &e., &c. (4). That the opportune granting of Home Rule to Canada and our other colonies has bound them in trustful loyalty to the British Empire. (5), That a coercive policy has been repeatedly exer- cised against Ireland—has again miserably failed and brought renewed disgrace upon the British Govern- ment. (6). That Mr. Gladstone's generous policy of con- ciliation is still available, and by the carnestco-operation of all sections of the Liberal Radical party', under his leadekg-ilit, a scheme of Home Rule could he carrl,44 that would satisfy Irelanci, wipe out the disgrace a Ce4iirles of mis-government, strengthen the unity of our empire, and merit the approbation of the whole civilized world. (7). That having as a re-united party conventionally performed an imperative duty, we shall be none the less, t all the Mere able to " Defend the Right "and protect the interests of every minority in Ireland whether relish. lous or political. (8). That Mr. Gladstone has A tCedea much to the expressed ttiiitOkiebt Liberals, arid that whateYer %Ali& Sett \*We ot Rome Rule may , be introdtleed *ill here to he discussed and voted upon by,the'elAdedrepreSentatives of the people in the House of COmMotis, and will be accepted or rejected by them upon its merits. (9). That the earnest cry to-day is for Domestic Legislation, and that those who still call themselves Liberals, yet callously stand aloof from re- union, are morally responsible to the working classes of this country for the prolonged absence of many much- needed reforms.—Your obedient servant, JAMES HAYSMAN (Liberal-Radical candidate, for Mile End). Finchley-road, London. •

Again, although it is called a renewal, it is only a way of putting it, for there is no such thing as a renewal in licenses. They are new every year, and are granted for "one year and no longer." Hence, at the year end the license is dead, and, unless another be obtained, the house must be closed as a public resort. Further it must be clear that, if the magistrates have power to grant, they have also the power to refuse, and, as that power has only been entrusted to them, as custodians of the people, it is within their right,when the people protest against a nuisance being placed at their doors. " Pluto " draws a comparison which, tells much more against his case, than for it. When " Pluto " buys a watch, it is then his own property absolutely. He can sell it, will it, give it away, or use it during his own lifetime, and then would become the property of his near- est relation. But in the case of a license, the analogy fails altogether. This right in the licensee is only for a year and no longer. He cannot sell it; nor will it, nor give it away, and when he dies, the license dies also, unless transferred, by the magistrates. The cry of robbery, is therefore all bosh. Again the indivi- dual who can't see it, is advised to look at the Bth Com- mandment. Why is not very apparent. It is said that there is only one step between the sublime and the ridiculous, and " Pluto " in his attempts to be funny has made that step. Pa-sing by the remainder of " Pluto's " letter as un- worthy of serious thought,allow me tothank you for your editorial of the previous week on the drink question, and to commend to your readers, a simple way, to deal with this growing evil. It is evident to all who take an in- terest in this question, that the magistrates,from a variety of causes, are unfitted to deal in a thorough manner with the licenses. The power should be given to the people, the people for whose convenience these licenses , are granted. The power should be given to them to "veto the licenses" if in their opinion, they are not wanted. It goes without saying that no political party will give this power, unless forced to do so by the popu- lar vote. It is time the temperance party realized their power; they are strong enough to turn any election which way they will. The party only needs banding together, with the determination not to rote for any one, who will not pledge himself to vote for the direct veto. being given to the people, over all licenses for the sale of intoxicating drink. The people may surely be entrusted to look after their own interests—and he who wilt not trust the people, ought not to be trusted.—Yours &c., PISTOL.

div.head: FEASTING RUNCORN OFFICIALS.
div.p: FEASTING RUNCORN OFFICIALS.

Sir,—After all, it appears that I ought to have consulted the oracle at the Town Hall before communicating with you, sir; but with all due deference to that important person I think it is doubtful whether he would have vouchsafed the information to so humble an individual as myself. I can quite picture the attitude be would have assumed, his apparent willingness to oblige, only that official etiquette would not allow him to comply with the request. This impression is confirmed by his letter, for he does not promise any particulars, but simply says any enquirer will be courteousiy received,which in my opinion means nothing. _ .

lam sorry if I have been led into any error in the statement I made, but my information was taken from the public proceedings of the Commissioners, and if that body, through any imtierfect system of its own, has not always given complete intelligence to the public the fault rests with them and not with me. However, be that as it may, I have some reason to doubt the absolute correctness of a part of your correspondent's figures. It is gratifying to note from the tone of Mr. Marshall's letter that the officials feel their position over the feast- ing business, and as that person appears anxious that the ratepayers should take his assuranca that the dinner did not cost more than 7s. each (by the way a good stiff price, and one which few persons would pay if the money had to come out their own pockets), what has he to say about the lunch, because he only disposes of £3 3s. out , of an expenditure of £5141. That would make what, with a touch of humour your correspondent "Dick Swiveller " called a "snack," more expensive than the dinner, and I will explain why. The officials of the Board, all told, number only eight, and the Assistant Overseer, makes nine. Of these, seven were employed at the election, so that there could not be several officials pre- sent at the dinner in addition to the seven. They do not exist ; at most there could be only two, but Mr. Mar- shall's remark" there were several officials present who had not been engaged" would lead one to believe, if one did not know the Board's servants, that, by including these with the workers, a number would be given which would bring the cost down to the figure he states. Mr. Marshall's explanation does not improve matters, and, do what he may, he cannot alter the amount, and this for the solids of life, no liquid being introduced. And now, Mr. Editor, I thank you for your courtesy. I hope the publicity which this subject has received will prevent in future such a state of affairs as was so graphi- cally portrayed by the Chairman, and that we shall have no more extravagant feasting of the officials at the rate- payers' expense. Runcorn, 13th October, 1890.
RATEPAYER.
THE LICENSING QUESTION.

Sir,—" Pluto," in your last issue, refers to "lovers of fair-play" as rejoicing at the decision of the Newton magistrates, in refusing to rob the proprietor of the Griffin Hotel of his license. Lovers of fair-play must be singularly dense if they see as he sees in the matter. As for the strictly honest people, they must be a peculiar set, and quite superlatively careful as regards "mine and thine." "Pluto" says the "magistrates refused to rob" &c. Were they asked to rob anyone? Again, can the refusal of the magistrates to grant a license be called robbery? If " Pluto " can prove that, then his
fortune is made,and the privileged beerseller has a better ease than he ever thought possible.

div.head: EX-SERGEANT SHAW: AN EXPLA_NATION
div.p: EX-SERGEANT SHAW: AN EXPLA_NATION
AND DEFENCE.
Sir,—Will you kindly grant me space in your valuable paper to give the reason why I left the Warrington Borough Police Force. . . .

I joined the Warrington Police on the 26th of May, 1831, and I was promoted to the rank of sergeant on the 6th of May, 1886. I was never reported during the whole of that time for anything, except for being late on one occasion at six o'clock in the morning, that being the first and only report against me. Since I was pro- moted to sergeant I have had two very severe illnesses. and Lam sorry to say that that is one of the greatest crimes that a policeman can commit, as I believe it is expected that he should be like a piece of iron or granite —proof against all weathers.

Now, f will try and explain the treatment I have received since being promoted to sergeant. I com- menced at 31s. per week, and I should have had 325. at the end of twelve months if free from report. That rise I did not receive until the 28th of February, 1889, about one year and nine months behind time. On the Bth of May, 1889, according to the rate of pay for sergeants, I was entitled to 335. per week. That rise, lam sorry to say, I had not received when I left the force; so you will see that out of the four years and three months that I was sergeant I lost is. per week for three years. After my last illness this year, I was told to look out for a fresh situation,which I refused to do, and I was then told that the Watch Committee would be asked to give me a month's notice. I, of course, defended myself, and said that I should attend the Committee, which I did, and I was at three meetings of the Committee before my case I came on. I defended my case there, and it was decided to adjourn it fora week ;so that the members could make Iprivate inquiries about me. I promised the gentlemen on the Committee that I would not go near the doctor; but the next day I received a note from the office order- ing me to see the doctor at 9.0 p.m. I thought it rather strange tkat such an order should be sent, after me mak- ing a promise not to go; but, of course, I obeyed the order, and went to the doctor, uho sounded me, and, seeing that I was not thoroughly recovered, he would not give me a final certificate for a month. At the next meeting of the Watch Committee when I was called into the room, I was told by his worship the Mayor, that he was sorry to say that they had considered ray case, and they had decided to reduce me to the rank of constable at 295. per week, as they considered I was not strong enough for sergeant. I was surprised ; and I am sure if I am not strong enongh for sergeant I am not for a constable. I told th 3 Committee so, and told them also that I could never submit to be reduced so long as I had committed no offence. They then gave me a week to consider whether I would resign or submit to be reduced. If I resigned, they would allow me to rOain my position until I had served my notice. I told theta then that my mind was fully made up, as I could not • think of serving as a constable after having held the position of sergeant. During the week that I had given MG to consider, I was advised not to resign, but simply to ps.i.t in a protest against the decision of the Watch Commit- tee. 'fp i46,7,r,;,74!s what I put in, and ttliq i§ wrmod 147 Fe4lß4Pili= (tom) Toliee Office, WarringtCh, August 14th, 1890. b•ir,—At the meeting of the Watch Committee held at the Town Hall, on Thursday, August 7th, 1890, it was decided to reduce me to the rank of constable at 295. per week, because I was not strong enough for sergeant. I wish to point out that if lam fit to do the duties of a constable that I must be able to perform the duties of sergeant, and I most respectfully beg to state to the Watch Committee and you that, if it is still decided to reduce me to the rank of constable without any charge against me. I would rather leave the force.—l am sir, your obedient servant,
P.S. 3, ROBERT SHAW.

Mr. Hunt, Chief Constable. Since joining the force, I have paid to the Superanua- tion Fund, al per cent, being deducted from my wages every week, and also paid to the Police Mutual Assur- ance Association. Altogether, I should think, without fear of contradiction, I have paid between £3O and £4O which, I suppose, according to the papers [cannot have refunded. I shall ever respect the gentlemen of the Council who have tried to get justice done me, as I am sure anyone will see that I have been got out of the force by anything but upright means. I could give a great many particulars which would surprise a great many people if the law allowed me, but I suppose a still tongue is the best now-a-days. Since severing my connection with the force, I believe the men were intending to make me a small present as a mark of respect, but I believe that was nipped in the bud and, of course, I have had to do without it. Not only has that been done away with, but the men dare not be seen speaking to me in the street which I consider is very hard. If I had been the greatest reprobate that ever walked, I could not be treated worse than I am being treated. lam very thankful to say that of the whole time I was on the force, I have not made one single enemy, and I shall always be treated with the greatest respect both by the ratepayers, and also the men on the force. If I had committed any crime, I should not think anything of the treatment that I am receiving, but I am glad to say that they cannot bring anything against me, except being straightforward, honest, and sober. If anything that is said against me other than what is true, I am quite able and willing to fight it out, either through the papers or on a public platform. I see in looking over the papers that a certain journal in the town is making me into a Radical. Now, Mr. Editor, I shall contradict that statement, and tell the person who put it in that he is rather too clever and knows more than I know myself, as I shall never be tied either to one party or the other. When Ido use my vote, it will be done by ballot, and no one will know how I have voted. Hoping you will be able to find room in your columns for this letter,—l remain, yours truly, Ex-Police Sergeant ROBERT SHAW. 105,-Manchester-rd., Warrington, October 15th, 1890.

div.head: POTTERIES AND MERSEY CANAL
div.p: THE POTTERIES AND MERSEY CANAL

The North Staffordshire Railway Company pro- prietors of the Trent and Mersey Canal, have pro- jected a scheme, which will cost .£300,000, to widen and deepen the canal between the Potteries and the Mersey. At present the canal carries barges of 25 tons burden. Under the proposed scheme flats of 60 tons burden, built to cross the Mersey, will run from Stoke-on-Trent to Runcorn in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal harbour there. The flats will then be unloaded at the side of sea-going ves- sels, and the cost and delay attending tranship- ment from the long and cranky barges at present in use, will be saved.

The new Portuguese Cabinet made its declaration of policy before the Chamber on Wednesday. The conven- tion with Great Britain is denounced, but the Ministers declare that they have no desire to abrogate the clauses which have been already put in force. ALLEGED THEFTS AT GOLBORNE.-At the Warrington County Police Court, on Wednesday, a man named Thos. Rothwell, was charged with stealing from the Victoria Hotel, Golborne, on the 9th inst., a metal coffee pot the property of Richard Dalton, which was valued at 55., also with stealing from a dwelling-house in Lowton-road on the same day, a silk handkerchief. As the police asked for a remand for a week, evidence in respect of the first charge only was given.—Mrs. Dalton, of the Victoria Hotel, said on the day in question the prisoner was in her house. The coffee pot was in her kitchen whilst prisoner was there, but when he he had gone she missed it. The case was accordingly remanded for a week.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 18, 1890.
BRIGGS, THE LANCASHIRE CRICKETER.

An excellent little work (price 6d.). has been published by Mr. John Heywood, with the title ”Cricket Celebrities of 1890." It gives a portrait and a sketch of each celebrity. The following is the account of John Briggs, the well-known Lancashire player:—Jack stands five feet five inches, but whether in his stocking feet or on stilts I don't know, but he's filled out a deal lately, and what is wanting in height is getting compensated for in girth, so that, all in all, he is not the least man we have on the cricket field. I am telling you what most people already know when I say that he was born in Nottinghamshire, the place of his debut on our planet being the home of many cricketers, Sutton-in-Ashfield. It seems to have been as easy raising cricketers in Sutton as it is growing potatoes in Ireland. There may be a bad crop some years, but the supply is generally equal to the demand. We will not allow Sutton-in-Ashfield to have all the honour of making Briggs a cricketer. It supplied the young plant,but Lancashire nurtured it, and our atmosphere and climate have done as well for its growth as that of Sutton could possibly have done, though it had no sweeter surroundings than the chemical air of sweet Widnes. Jack was born on October 3rd, 1862, and was only fourteen when he took his first professional engagement. This was at Hornsea, in '76. I don't know much of what he did in that engagement, hut in '7B we found him doing good business as pro, for the Liverpool Northern Club,•and it was there he first enlisted the attention of the Lancashire Committee, I believe it was It. G. Barlow who first preached his merits, and for Bar- low to say something in hie favour meant some- thing in those days. That ancient institution, the Colts' matches, at Manchester, proved to be young Briggs's introduction to a critical public, and the Notts boy pleased the Lancashire boys immensely, so much so that he was booked for the first county match of the year 1879. It was rather singular, but, as a fact, the first county he played against was the county of his birth, and no young professional could have had his nerves more severely tested than he had. The weather was cold and cheerless, the wickets slow and difficult, but against such fine bowlers as Alfred Shaw, poor Fred Morley, Barnes, and Flowers, this budding plant blossomed success- fully, and made the highest score on his side, viz., 36. To be a successful county man you must be something more than a promising bat, and this Briggs was, for he proved himself exceptionally smart in the field and a decent change bowler. Who, then, could fail to predict for him a great future? a prediction that has been verified beyond all anti- cipation, and scores have been the times that he has carried the Lancashire crowd away in admiration. In 1881 he did some smart things for his adopted county. His first essay that year was really the pluckiest of the lot, though not his highest score, and to earn fame and distinction you need not necessarily make phenomenal figures. The match in question was against M.C.C., and when Lancashire seemed all but beaten, Briggs came to the rescue with as useful an innings ever played in a match. It amounted to only 40 runs, but it turned apparent defeat into victory, and Lancashire won by two wickets. Then, on another occasion he made 52 against Surrey, a performance at that time very much appreciated. The season of 'B3 was a very successful one for him. He made 55 in his opening match against Derbyshire. and in the return against the same shire he made 60. His plucky hitting, too, against Surrey in the second innings at Old Trafford did much to turn a game which, when he came in. looked most hopeful for Surrey. In 1884 he opened the season with 74 against M.C.C., and thfs year saw him run up his first century for Lan- cashire, scoring 112 against Derbyshire without giv- ing a chance. Finer innings have not often been witnessed than his 75 not out against Yorkshire, in Allan Hill's benefit match, the total reaching only

170. In 1884 he was included in some of the repre- sentative matches, playing six times against the Australians. He assisted the players both at Sheffield and the Oval, and played for the North at Manchester, also for the Players against the Gentle- men. At the end of that season he paid his first visit to Australia, and did exceedingly well on one occasion, scoring 121 in brilliant style. It would be going over well-beaten ground to describe his latter career. As a bowler, batter, and fielder he has made himself a name that cannot be beaten, and no repre-

sen—tative English team would be complete wittiout him. Unfortunately an accident in the Yorkshire match at Old Trafford this season rendered him hors de combat for a considerable time, and he could not appear in some of the big matches of the year, but previous to his accident he displayed all his old brilliance in every department of the game, and his enforced idleness through the accident was a severe blow to cricket generally, but more especially to Lancashire. Briggs is a very genial young fellow, 4.8 popular as the best of them, and never makes his appearance without receiving a welcomipg her.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. That the ratepayers of Widnes will by a vast majority declare in favour of incorporation when the question is put to them within the next few days. That the statement made by Mr. Allen, the clerk, to the effect that on this years estimates, had the town being a borough the rate would have been 2s. 51d. instead of 2s. 6d. in the .£ as at present, will vitae many waverera to give their vote for a Dilu- ter.

That as Mr. Carey observed, there was no reason why there should be more extravagance under a , corporation than under a local board, but with the increase of dignity conferred upon the town by mayor, aldermen, and councillors. there will be a desire to complete the public offices by the addi- tion of the Town Wall, which was originally esti- mated to cost about £7,000, and this, if carried out, will mean a penny or two extra on the rate. That the Town Hall is much needed for many reasons, and nobody would grumble at the extra charge entailed. That there are already inquiries Ps to who will be the first six aldermen and echo answers " Who ? " That Mr. Gossage will undoubtedly be the first mayor, and it is to be hoped that ere long we shall see his portrait alongside that of his father, the late Mr. Wm. Gossage in the Council Chamber. That it is satisfactory to learn that the Health Committee are taking measures to prevent, if pos- sible, the nuisances which arise from several of the works. That the Board were wise in not interfering with the question of hawking, over which it appeared they had little control, and we shall have free trade in fish and vegetables for some time to come. That the University Extension Lectures on politi- cal economy made a successful start last week, when a large audience listened to an able and highly interesting lecture on" Wealth and Wages" by Mr. Smith. That political economy is a question affecting all classes of society, and none more so than the work- ing-men of the town, who would gain valuable knowledge by attending the course.

div.head: PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.
div.p: PROPOSED INCORPORATION OF WIDNES.

The Local board of Wickes having decided on a house to house canvass to ascertain the feeling of the inhabitants on the question of incorporation, a few facts as to the town will be read just now with more than ordinary interest. Half a century kz) there was scarcely a population worth mentioning in the place. Somewhere at ut the year 1847, however, alkali manufacturers fixed upon it as a seat for that industry, and now it can very properly be described as the home of the trade in &igland. An enormous business is now carried on in this sort of manufacture the carry- ing facilities from the town being excellent, both by rail and water. This growth of prosperity of necessity brought in its wake a growth of populat;on, which is now variously cstimated at from 31,000 to 35,000, and is considered to be rapidly on the increase. In 1881 it was only calculated at about 24,000, and in 1888 it had jumped up to g 9,723, The rateable value in 1881 yrs.: £101,943, and at the beginning of the present year it was £132,885. Purbher, it is calculated that during the last three months it has been increased by some £B,OOO. Some years ago a desire began to be manifested in some quarters that Widnes should attain the status of a municipal borough, and as the accomplishment of that desire is thought to be a matter of the near future, it may not be uninteresting to briefly sketch the various movements that have been made in the direction of securin,ga charter of incorporation. The initiative was taken about seven years ago by Dr. O'Keeffe, a member of the Local Board,who has all along been one of the most ardent champions of the movement. At that time, when Major Cross was chairman of the board, a numer- ously-signed requisition in favour of incorporation was drawn up, and a meeting of the ratepayers was sum- moned for the purpose of considering the matter. At that meeting, which was held in the Drill Hall, there was only a scanty attendance of the public, and the proposal for incorporation, as 'well as a proposal to adopt the Free Libraries Act, were for the time being shelved. About two years later, soon after Mr. Gossage, who retains the position, had become chairman of the board, similar steps were again taken, and on this occa- sion the town secured the manifest advantages of an adoption of the Free Libraries Act. The proposition to incorporate the the town was negatived by a smaU majority. Yet, again, in the Jubilee year, the matter was once more under discussion, and the members of the Widnes Ratepayers' Association joined in the agita- tion. Mr. Christie, the secretary of that organisation, wrote to several towns that had recently being incorpor- ated, mostly with a view of getting information as to how the rates of those towns had been affected, and in most cases, the replies were favourable to incorpora- tion. Ultimately, to bring matters up to date, this and other information was about two months ago communicated to the local board by Dr. O'Keeffe. At a recent meeting of the Board the subject , was again introduced on the reading of a letter from the ' Widnes Owners' and Occupiers' Association, who asked that the matter should not be decided upon until full in- formation had been obtained, and a poll of the inhabi- tants taken. After some discussion, it was resolved to obtain further information. The Local Board, on Tues.- day last, decided to canvass the ratepayers on the sub- ject, and there is reason to think their opinion will be favourable to the scheme. It is proposed that, in the event of a charter being obtained, the new borough of Widnes shall be divided into six wards, with three coun- cillors and one alderman to represent each. In other matters Widnes has been among the category of go-ahead places, and there seems little reason to doubt now, that incorporation will soon follow. It has a fairly good town hall, but with the exception of that building and perhaps one or two of the churches, there is little to call for notice from an architectural point of view. The buildings are more of a useful than of an ornamental character. There is an admirable accident hospital, which in a manufacturing centre like Widnes is of inesti- mable service ; and also an infectious diseases hospital. The latter was only erected a few years ago, after an in- vasion of smallpox had proved a most potent argument in its favour. Another progressive step which has just been taken is the adoption of the Technical Instruction Act, and the taking over of the Widnes Science and Art Schools, which hitherto have been supported by volun- tary contributions and Government grant. The science and art schools were commenced some 14 or 15 years ago, and the school buildings and property are equal in value to about £7OO. The amount of rate which the Local Board have power to levy for the support of these tech- nical schools cannot exceed id. in the £.

Thomas P. Murphy has just died in Boston Hospital penniless. He was organist of the chapel on the estate of the late Earl of Gainsborough, and married the Earl's, daughter against the family wishes, He took her to , America, where she died after a miserable married life.

div.head: NUISANCE OF THE INTERCEPTING
div.p: THE NUISANCE OF THE INTERCEPTING

DEPOTS. The following correspondence, which we have been requested to publish, shows that the Municipal Election will not be allowed to pass without candi- dates being called upon to express a definite opinion upon the nuisance of the Intercepting Depots. Mr. Blackhurst, it will be seen, pledges himself dis- tinctly upon the question, which is a most import- ant one as affecting the health and comfort of the inhabitants :

Lythgoes Lane, Warrington, Oct. 16th, 1890. Dear Sir,—ln view of the approaching Municipal Election for St. John's Ward, for whichyou are a candi- date, I venture to ask you if you are satisfied that the inhabitants of the Ward are justified in objecting very strongly to the continued working of the Intercepting Depot there; and whether you will be prepared to help them in their endeavour to suppress the present very serious nuisance, by voting for closing the place as a Nightsoil Depot, if necessary,--Yours truly, JOHN PLATT. IGKaorge Blaekhurst, Esq.

10 Sankey Street, Warrington, Oct. 16th, 1890. Dear reply to yours of to-day's date, I may say that if lam returned to the Town Council as the repre- sentative of &. John's Ward, I am quite prepared to vote for the closing of the Intercepting Depot, if the nuisance caused therdrom is not entirely suppressed. lam of opinion that the complaints of the inhabitants as to the nuisance are quite justifiable, and will do all in my power in assisting them In doing away with it.—l am, yours truly, GEO. BLACKHURST. John Platt, 3,1%

We have rneived a letter from Mr. Longton, too late for publication, in which he states that he has the authority of Councillors Fleming, Shaw Green, and Percival, and Mr. John Roberts, for saying that they are prepared to vote, if returned to the Council, for the removal of the Depots, if they cannot be made inoffensive o the inhabitants.

div.head: WARRINGTON MAN APPOINTED TO
div.p: A WARRINGTON MAN APPOINTED TO
A RESPONSIBLE POST.
We take the annexed from "The Brighouse Echo." The Mr. Tunstall referred to is a Warrington gentle- man—the brother of Messrs. Thomas, and T. L. I•Tunstall . .

We hasten, amongst a large number of friends, to con- gratulate Mr. Wilmott Tunstall, of Bradford-road, Brig- house, upon his success in obtaining the appointment of general manager for Messrs. Jonas Brook and Bros., the well known and old established firm of sewing cotton manufacturers, of Meltham Mills, near Huddersfield, and Spring-lane Mills, Holmfirth. Mr. Tunstall received news of his appoirtment on Tuesday morning, and since that time has been the recipient of the kindly congratu- lations of his friends. We understand, there were no less than 260 applications for the position. Out of this num- ber, Mr. Armitage, a member of the firm, with whom the appointment had been left, made a selection of four candidates, amongst whom, of course, was Mr. Tunstall. Mr. Armitage declined to make the final selection, which was left with the whole of the partners, whose choice fell upon Mr. Tunstall. There were three or four inter- views, and Mr. Tunstall placed before the firm the most unexceptional references. It will be at once understood by all who know the firm of Messrs. Brook, that the position is a very responsible one ; indeed, it ranks amongst the leading positions of cotton mill management in England. The works consist of several very large blocks of buildings, containing 95,000 spindles, and giv- ing employment to close upon 2,000 workpeople. The firm manufacture sewing thread from the raw cotton, and have their own bleaching and dyeing departments; over all of which Mr. Tunstall will have the management. The firm have also their own gas works. A salary of £l,OOO a year is attached to the appointment, and there also goes with it a first-class modern residence at Mel- them. Mr. Tunstall has been at Brighouse for seven years, as manager at Wood Vale Mills, Thornhill Briggs, for Messrs. Blackburn, Smith, and Co. of Halifax. He Is a native of Warrington, but learnt his business with the late Mr. Esau Hanson, cotton spinner and doubler, of Halifax. After leaving Mr. Hanson's service, Mr. Tun- stall engaged with Messrs. Blackburn, Smith, and Co., and for 'five years was manager for that firm at Dapper Mill, Wheatley, near Halifax. On March 6th, 1883, Dapper Mill was destroyed by fire, and on the 28th of the same month, Mr. Tunstall came to Brighouse and took charge of Wood Vale Mill for the same firm. Mr. Tunstall is well known as a teacher of cotton spinning in connection with the City and Guilds of London Institute, having conducted classes at Halifax, Huddersfield, Brig- house, Elland, and West Vale. His new appointment will compel him to relinquish cotton class teaching, and the classes he has already formed for the ensuing session, will have to be handed over to other teachers. The class at the Bridge End Institute' Brighouse, which now num- bers 42 students, and is the largest class formed in cotton manufacture between Brighouse and Oldham, is to be conducted by Mr. E. H. Sugden, of Brighouse, who has applied for a teacher's certificate ; the Huddersfield and Halifax classes are to be conducted by Mr. John Beswick, Jun., of Sowerby Bridge ; the class at West Vale will probably be undertaken by Mr. John Ainley, of Lock- wood. Mr. Tunstall expects to enter upon his new ap- pointment at Meltham in the course of about three weeks.

div.head: PASSION PLAY OF 1890.
div.p: THE PASSION PLAY OF 1890.

11. FROM BETHANY TO GETHSEMANE. Cairo-street Chapel was again crowded at the special service on Sunday evening last when the Rev. Frank R. Freeston delivered a second short ad- dress on the Passion Play. He began by briefly describing the village of Ober-Ammergau, and the lovely valley of the Ammer in which it lies, and considered that this beautiful Bavarian district was worthy of greater admiration that had yet been bestowed upon it. He then proceeded to describe the large wooden theatre in which the play took place, the unusually spacious stage on which it was performed,and the simple, yet most effective scenery by which it was made so picturesque and real. Only half the theatre was roofed over, the other halt, including the stage, being in the open air. This imparted to the perfermance an indescribable charm and freshness, and rendered entirely needless the gas jets, footlights electric gleams, and other stage artifices of an ordinary theatre ; all was genuine, simple, and natural. The play itself, he characterised as a skilful and unique combination of oratorio, tableau and drama. It en- deavoured to represent, historically and scripturally, the life of Christ during his last week on earth, and theretore was compelled to portray the most solemn scenes in Christian history. The music, though not am- bitious either in composition or execution, was yet most impressively rendered by a choir of guardian angels, called the chorus, whose office was to introduce the vari- ous tableaux and explain itheir connection with the play. The tableaux consisted of scenes from the Old Testament supposed to be prophetic of Christ, and were masterpieces of grouping, colouring, and motionless effect. In one, which alone he would single out for special mention, 400 peasants, including 150 children, were placed in position, at a few moments notice, with all the precision and symmetry of a canvas picture. As to the scenes themselves, or representation roper—no weak words ot his could convey an adequate idea of their marvellous power and majestic beauty. The 'plot" followed closely the Gospel lines and the words likewise sc far as possible, but additions to each had been freely made and without distressing results. As there were just twenty-five of these telling scenes, and as the whole play took eight hours to perform, he must be con- tent that night to refer to the twelve which comprised the first part of the play. These included amongst others The Entry of Christ into Jerusalem, The Cleansing of the Temple, The Council of High Priests, Christ at Bethany, Mary anointing Christ's feet, Christ weeping over Jerusa- lem, The Last Supper, The Agony in Gethsemane, and The Betrayal by Judas. After rapidly indicating in order the chief features of these various scenes, Mr. Freeston remarked that from beginning to end, from Bethany to Gethsemane, they produced a ceaseless series of solemn impressions. He should never forget the deep hush which passed over that vast assembly when the second signal gun was fired, nor the intensely reverent expectation with which was awaited the appearance of the Christ. Every eye was turned upon him, every head upraised to catch the first accents of his gentle voice, while the brightest morning sunlight flooded the scene and filled all the place with its glory. Everyone seemed afraid to move lest they might lose a word or a look. And the whole effect was most imposing. Let them place themselves in imagination near the back of that theatre in Ober- A mmergan. As they looked over the heads of over four thousand of their fellowmen, their thoughts would be turned to the world of to-day and the manifold needs of humanity at large. Let them then lift their eyes but a little way to the great Christian tragedy there played before them, and their thoughts would RAPILAEL'S ALMANAC FOR 1891. div.head: WINALLIE CYCLE COMPANY.
div.p: THE WINALLIE CYCLE COMPANY.
• INPENDING LITIGATION.

There has-1;e-eiTit—gOOd deal of talk in the town about the formation, the brief working, and the somewhat sudden failure, of the Winallie Cycle Company. It is a matter of course to say that a considerable number of shareholders are greatly dissatisfied with the turn of events, and some of them do not hesitate to say the condition and pros- pects of the Company have proved to be the reverse of what they anticipated. One of the shareholders, who has not yet paid up, has declined to respond to the call of the Receiver who has the estate in hand now that the Company is in liquidatiox. This shareholder believes that he has good grounds for refusing to pay, and has determined that, at any rate, the matter shall be tested in the County Court on Thursday next, the claim upon him, which is for £45, bringing the case within the jurisdiction of that Court. It is not unlikely that 1 his worship the Mayor (Alderman Francomb) will be subpcened amongst other witnesses to give I evidence, and it is expected that there will be some interesting if not startling revelations.

div.head: FRODSIIAM.
div.p: FRODSIIAM.

FOREIGN MISSIOWS.—On Sunday, sermons were preached on behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society, in the Trinity Chapel, by the Rev. P. Pizey, morning and evening, and on Wednesday evening the annual public meeting was held, presided over by Mr. E. J. Guest, J.P., of Helsby. From the report read by the Rev. F. F. Edmunds, it appeared that of the £B3 16s. 10d. contri- buted by the circuit to the Foreign Mission and Zenana Funds, the Frodsham friends had contributedL43 6s. sd. Addresses were delivered by the Chairman, the Rev. P. Pizey, and the deputation, the Rev. G. Parkyn, formerly army chaplain In Egypt, at the conclusion of which votes of thanks were accorded to them. . . . . .

Nunn Cuuncn SERVICES.—The harvest thanksgiving services in connection with the Frodsham Parish were continued on Sunday morning and evening, when the Vicar (the Rev. H. B. Fflogg, M.A.) preached. The offertories amounted to £7 103. A special service was held in the church in the afternoon, which was in part a flower service, when the Rev. J. D. Ringrose pn,eached. £3 4s. id. was the amount of offertories received, and goes to the Chester Infirmary Fund, with the sum previously received, and £2 received from friends who were absent from the services, making a gross total of £l7 15s. 6d. There was a large congregation at each of the services, but particularly the evening service, when the church was crowded. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—A conver- sazione was held in the Trinity Schoolroom, Frodsham, last evening week, when the President (the Rev. P. Pizey) occupied the chair. The programme, consisted of an en- joyable address by til. Chairman, short explanatory lec- tures on a collection of autumn flowers, which had been sent by Messrs. Dickson, Chester, and a number of botanical specimens gathered by one of the members of , the class dutiog tha recent excursion to Delamera Forest, together with a selection of vocal and instrumental music. Besides the foregoing, there were some half dozen micro- scopes, with interesting objects on view, and during an interval refreshments were served round. There were a large number of members and friends in attendance.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

A meeting Of this Board was held in the Sessions Room, Daresbury, on Thursday, Mr. J. C. Parr (chairman), presiding. There was a good attend- ance of members. THE LATE SURVEYOR.—The Chairman read a letter from Mr. Feerman, the late surveyor of the Board,thank- ing them for the generous manner in which they had compensated him for the extra work that had fallen upon him, through the making of the Ship Canal. A COMPLAINT FROM WESTON.—A letter was read from Mr. Fitton, shopkeeper, of Weston, complaining of the quantity of road sweepings being placed opposite his premises.—Thei attention of the surveyor was called to the matter. Tux MORRIS BROOK NEW ROAD.—The Clerk reported that he had written to Mr. Leader Williams, as to a de. viation from the plan in the making of the new road at Mortis Brook. Mr. Leader Williams in reply, pointed out that the Canal Company could vary any work within their limits of deviation. He was informed that the road,as now made,met the wishes of the persons who mainly used it. The Ship Canal Committee had con- sidered the matter, and inspected the road. Mr. Hunter attended the meeting of the Committee, on behalf of the Ship Canal Company, and said they had made the devia- tion with the cognisance of the late surveyor, and they could not now alter it, as the land over which the road was originally intended to run, had been re-sold by the Company. The Committee, after a long discussion, agreed that if the Company would give two strips of land on the left hand side of the road, they would recommend the Boatcl to accept the deviation. This proposal having been placed before Mr. Leader Williams, he wrote that the Highway Board had no claims on the Company for the two strips of land. He would, however, look into the matter on the spot. It was decided by the Board to again communicate with Mr. Leader Williams on the matter, it being stated that Mr. Peennan, the late sur- veyor, denied having given any consent to the devia- tion. THE Nsw ROADS NEAR LOWER WALTON.—A meeting of the Ship Canal Committee of the Board was held at Lower Walton on the sth August when the Canal Com- pany were represented by Mr. 0. G. Brooke and Mr. F. Monks, the complainant in the case, was also present. Mr. Brooke pointed out to the Committee the original position of the road (which was changed to its present one at the suggestion of the Committee) and explained that if it had remained in that position it would not have been Ipposite the road from Hill Cliffe, but would have had an awkward turn. The Committee agreed that the road in the present position was much better than in the former one, but that it would be a great boon to the travelling public if the terminus of the intended new road on the east side, and the road from Hill Cliffe could be widened as suggested by Mr. Monks, if the Board could acquire the land to do so. It was decided by the Board that the Surveyor should corn- munilate with the County Surveyor on the subject, and then report to the Board. ALTERATIONS OF ROADS.—The Ship Canal Committee had considered some slight alterations which the Ship Canal Company proposed to make to the lines of the approaches to the roads at or near Latchford Station in , order to meet the requirements of Mr. Stevenson, the engineer to the London and N. W. Railway Company. The C.mmittee,being of opinion that the proposed alter- ations-would be a great improvement,they recommended the Board not to interfere in the matter. A proposed slight alteration to the levels of the new road across Arpley meadows was also considered and the Committee again recommended the Board not to interfere in the mattar.—The report of the Committee was adopted. This was the principal business.

A verdict of wilful murder was returned by the coroner's jury on Thursday night at Holloway, London, against Henry Thomas, a carpenter. He became ac- quainted with a woman named Annie Smith, and she permitted him to waste her property. When he had spent her money and she found it impossible to supply him with further funds, he pulled her out of bed and, it is alleged, placed his foot upon her. It is also said that he deliberately upset a paraffin lamp, intending to cause her death. Anyhow the woman was found near the bed- room door with her clothes on fire, and was so saverely burnt that she afterwards died.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER TRADE, PRIDAY.—No change of moment has heen noticeable in any department of the market, and the business put through has not exceeded very moderate dimen- sions. Cotton is Rot brisk, but a better tone has been de- veloped since the opening, and the estimate of sales has been raised from 7,000 to 8,000 bales. Yarns are just as firm as they were, and there is no great eagerness to buy. Even for wefts there is no longer any rush to get hold of a few skips, and looms are in many cases allowed to stand waiting for delivery of yarns already bought. Bundles are steady, but trade is I very moderate at quotations. In cloth things are no better. LIVRIIPOOL PROVISIONS, PRIDAY.—In oeef good parcels are firmly held, but the demand is only moderate. Pork shows no change in value, and there is not much doing. Bacon continues to meet an improve 1 inquiry, and, with ad- vices from America of lighter shipments, all descriptions are firmer in tone, long and short boneless being held for an ad- vance of CRI per cwt. Hams and shoulders are also firmer. Cheese remains quietly steady. Butter is not quotably al- tered ; and lard has a sluggish sale at unchanged .rates.

Why is it that some people can scarcely venture out of doors during damp and foggy weather? It is becanaa that owing either to a naturally delicate constitution or the neglect of proper precaution in time, they are liable at the least exposure to draughts, winds, or damp, to catch a cold which will develope into a cough. Influenza, Asthma, Bronchitis, Inflammation, or even Consumption ! Why is it that others either can not or dare not enjoy the pleasures on the table, that partaking of necessarY food is impossible, or the free indulgence of their taste results in horror which the bravest shrink from ? It Is because they are troubled with Indigestion in some form or other, whether it goes under the name of DyspePaia, Flatulence, Bilious, Head-ache, Loss of Appetite, or any other form of that malady. WHY is it that others again arie dispirited, nervous, melancholy, always look upon the dark side, and regard everything through the coloured spectacles of a morbid imagination? It is because they sufferfrom a disordered Liver, which brings nervous headache, sleeplessness, jaundice, bile, low spirits, confirmed melancholy, ann other horror in its train.

THE SUPPOSED MURDER AT ASHTON- UNDER-LYNE. At the adjourned inquest at Ashton-under-Lyne, on Wednesday, on the 14ody of Henry Nally, who was found outraged and murdered in a field on September the 29th last, there was no fresh evidence to adduce,the police be- ing unable to obtain the slightest clue to the perpetrators of the crime. The jury consequently returned a verdict of wilful murder against some person or persons un- known.

DEATH OF PROFESSOR THOROLD ROGERS. Mr. J. E. Thorold Rogers, M.A., professor of political economy at the University of Oxford, died at his resi- dence, Beaumont-st., Oxford, on Monday. He had been in failing health for some time past. He was born at Westmeon in 1823, and graduated at Magdalen in 1849. He became a clergyman of the Church of England, but reling,uished orders to enter Parliament, which he did in 1880 for Southwark, which borough he represented down to 1886. He was an advanced Liberal, and was the author of numerous works on economic subjects.

SUICIDE FROM CLIFTON BRIDGE. Another suicide took place on Friday morning from Clifton Suspension Bridge, when a man unknown leaped from the stretcher. BRITISH SHIP LOST, WITH PART OF CREW. Lloyd's agent at Hiogo telegraphs . that the British ship Lizzie C. Troop, from Nagasaki for Paget Sound, is totally lost at Loochoo. Part of the crew are saved. MURDER IN IRELAND. Castlebar correspondent telegraphs :—A man, named Thomas Nolan, was found dead on the road, near Castle. bar, yesterday, with his skull fractured and other injuries, having evidently been murdered. There is no explanation of the crime, and no arrest has been made. ANOTHER LONDON FIRE. A destructive fire occurred yesterday morning at the premises of Messrs. John BridgmAn and Son coach- makers, in Brownlow Mews, near Gray's Inn-road, Bloomsbury, London. Messrs. Bridgman's premises were burnt out, the loss being estimated at between £3,000 and £4,000, which is not covered by insurance. At six o'clock the progress of the fire was checked. SHIPPING CASUALTIES. The steamer Great Western, from Dublin for More. cambe, has landed her cattle at Holyhead. Yesterday the barque Ephrath was towed into Dover damaged, by e,ollison with the schooner Our Nellie. The schooner Hannah Jane, of Portmadoc was tun- ing into Holyhead harbour for shelter from the gale, on Thursday night, and collided with the Elizabeth Alice. Both are damaged.
